# Overview: What Electrodialysis Is and Why It Matters

Electrodialysis (ED) is an electrically driven membrane separation process that uses ion‑exchange membranes (anion‑ and cation‑selective) arranged in stacks to remove dissolved salts and other ions from water by transporting them toward oppositely charged electrodes under an applied electric field, concentrating them in specific compartments while desalinating the “diluate” streams <cite id="5fa029ef-0">Electrodialysis is one of the common membrane technologies used for water desalination, with advantages, limitations, and challenges discussed in a recent review</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Electrodialytic systems comprise ion exchange membranes and associated phenomena; recent developments include electroconvection, pulsed fields, electrodeionization, and shock electrodialysis</cite>. ED is commercially deployed, with market activity spanning decades and a growing pipeline of sustainable strategies and circular‑economy applications <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Market overviews show global revenues, manufacturers, and trends, linking electrodialytic phenomena to sustainable strategies and eco‑efficient integrations</cite>.

Electrodeionization (EDI) extends ED by integrating ion‑exchange resins and membranes in flow channels with applied electric fields to continuously regenerate resins and drive ion transport, producing ultrapure water often used as polishing after reverse osmosis (RO) or as a standalone deionization unit <cite id="d311a19b-0">EDI employs ion‑exchange membranes and resin particles under an applied electric field, enabling continuous regeneration and conductivity supplementation for ultrapure water production</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI substitutes mixed‑bed ion exchange in boiler makeup treatment and is essential for polishing RO permeate to resistivity >17 MΩ·cm</cite>. Shock electrodialysis (shock ED) is an emerging variant that leverages electric fields and ion concentration polarization to concentrate and remove specific ions, including radionuclides, with recent demonstrations using ion‑exchange membranes and porous separators <cite id="5fa029ef-2">Shock electrodialysis induces ion transport and separation via polarization to remove radionuclides; earlier work proposed its suitability over traditional precipitation/adsorption, using ion‑exchange membranes and porous separators</cite>.

# Device Configuration and Operating Modes

In ED stacks, alternating anion‑ and cation‑exchange membranes form selective compartments where cations and anions migrate toward cathode/ anode, respectively, into concentrate channels; diluate channels thereby lose ions and are desalinated <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Principles and state‑of‑the‑art membrane phenomena, including limiting current density, electroconvective vortices, and pulsed fields, are associated with ED stacks and transport equations</cite>. Operation can be direct current (DC) or pulsed/alternating fields; pulsed fields can enhance mass transfer and mitigate concentration polarization, with electroconvective vortices aiding transport near membranes <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Electroconvective vortices and pulsed‑electric fields are discussed as mechanisms to enhance mass transfer in electrodialytic systems</cite>.

EDI integrates flow‑through ion‑exchange resins between membrane pairs in channels; applied potential drives ions from feed/leach streams into adjacent concentrate compartments while resins are continuously regenerated electrochemically, reducing chemical regeneration needs compared to mixed beds <cite id="d311a19b-0">EDI continuously regenerates resins and supplements conductivity, enabling ultrapure water production</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI downstream of RO/polishing to ultra‑low conductivity; replaces mixed beds due to avoidance of chemical regeneration issues and complex operations</cite>. Current research also explores shock ED cells and hybrid ED‑filtration integrations for sustainability and performance tailoring <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Applications include shock electrodialysis and ED with filtration membranes, with sustainable strategies proposed for circular economy contexts</cite>.

# Transport Concepts: Current Efficiency, Limiting Current, and Selectivity

Current efficiency (CE) quantifies the fraction of applied charge used to transport target ions; it is commonly computed from measured current and ion transfer equivalents using Faraday’s constant and stack geometry, and is central to assessing energy use and applicability <cite id="faf97161-1">Current utilization (current efficiency, Coulombic/charge efficiency) is the ratio of current used to effectively separate salt ions to total applied current, typically >90% in desalination processes</cite> <cite id="faf97161-2">CE compares moles of ion transferred to Faradays consumed; it indicates how effectively ions are transported per applied current</cite>. CE depends strongly on membrane selectivity, pH, and hydrodynamics; scaling and hydroxide deposition at membranes, leakage via electroosmosis, and transport through membrane “leakage” channels all reduce CE and ion removal <cite id="faf97161-3">Current efficiency decreases with more cell pairs and longer operation; fewer cell pairs give higher current efficiency when metal removal >95%; losses arise from membrane selectivity changes, scaling, leakage, and osmosis/electroosmosis; exceeding limiting current density causes polarization and rapid pH swings leading to hydroxide scaling</cite>.

The limiting current density (LCD) is set by diffusion‑controlled transport of counterions from feed to concentrate streams; simple models such as the Lévêque approximation express LCD in terms of ion valence, bulk concentration, membrane and solution transport numbers, diffusion coefficient, and membrane conductivity <cite id="faf97161-4">Theoretical LCD can be calculated with Lévêque equations using counterion charge, concentration, effective transport numbers in membrane and solution, diffusion coefficient, and Faraday’s constant</cite>. Exceeding LCD accelerates polarization, pH swings, and scaling, reducing efficiency and membrane lifetime unless mitigated by hydrodynamics, pH buffering, or bipolar membranes to route non‑target ions to alternate streams <cite id="faf97161-3">Exceeding LCD increases solution electrical resistance, drops process efficiency, and induces rapid pH changes that cause hydroxide deposition and scaling</cite>.

# Performance Metrics and Benchmarks

Energy consumption is typically reported as specific electrical energy (kWh/m³) or normalized by salinity and current density. For ED/EDI systems treating brackish groundwater or low‑salinity streams, reported specific energy consumption spans roughly 0.39–2.11 kWh/m³ for EDI in power‑sector case studies, with ED often lower depending on stack/membrane/resin design and duty cycle <cite id="d311a19b-1">Specific energy consumption of EDI commonly ranges from 0.39 to 2.11 kW·m⁻³; EDI’s use of membranes and resins lowers resistance of deeply deionized water relative to electrochemical competitors</cite>. EDI can achieve near‑complete desalination (99.9999%) to produce water with resistivity >17 MΩ·cm, whereas two‑pass RO struggles to reach comparable purity and requires more energy and lower recovery; EDI is often unavoidable to reach <0.0625 µS·cm⁻¹ conductivity targets <cite id="d311a19b-1">Theoretical and practical EDI desalination efficiency can reach 99.9999%, producing water with resistivity exceeding 17 MΩ·cm, outperforming two‑pass RO in both quality and energy recovery for sub‑16 MΩ·cm targets</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI completes polishing after RO and avoids chemical regeneration complexities; two‑pass RO is not cost‑effective for producing water better than 16 MΩ·cm</cite>.

Measured current efficiencies vary by configuration and ion. In a food‑solution demineralization stack, an averaged current efficiency of ~26% was achieved using potassium as the tracer, with energy consumption ~14.9 Wh per test; lower values than literature were attributed to migration into a rinse stream and geometry, underscoring the sensitivity of CE to stack design and measurement boundaries <cite id="faf97161-0">Averaged current efficiency of 26.36 ± 1.79% and energy consumption ~14.90 ± 0.30 Wh were observed; lower efficiencies than prior hCEM work were linked to cation migration into a rinse compartment and stack geometry</cite>. In heavy‑metal‑containing wastewater, current efficiency around 16–17% at >95% separation was observed for 5–9 cell‑pair stacks, declining with more pairs and longer operation, highlighting a trade‑off between throughput and charge usage and the need to optimize current density and hydrodynamics to minimize cost <cite id="faf97161-3">Current efficiency decreased with cell‑pair number and operating time; with 5–9 pairs, CE ~16–17% coincided with >95% separation; fewer pairs improved current efficiency due to reduced stepwise performance loss</cite>.

# Applications Across Water Treatment and Resource Recovery

Electrodialytic processes are widely applied in desalination and demineralization for power sector makeup, industrial process water, and alternatives to mixed‑bed demineralizers, achieving stringent conductivity targets that exceed RO permeate alone <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI integrates after UF/RO to meet stringent boiler makeup limits; it completes softening and heavy metal removal and cannot be simply substituted by two‑pass RO</cite>. EDI’s continuous electrochemical regeneration of resins has made it a commercial mainstay for ultrapure water, with documented replacement of mixed beds in centralized plants <cite id="d311a19b-0">EDI is commercially used for ultrapure water; resin immobilization in ionomer‑binder wafers improved desalination rates and reduced energy at dilute salt concentrations</cite>.

Beyond drinking water, ED/EDI are used for nutrient recovery from wastewater, where systematic studies quantify how operating factors and membrane choices affect electrodialytic efficiency and cost, providing decision frameworks for designers and policymakers <cite id="5fa029ef-3">A systematic review classifies essential factors affecting ED efficiency in nutrient recovery and discusses operating challenges and costs</cite>. In specialty applications, ED variants like shock ED have demonstrated continuous removal of radionuclides by exploiting ion concentration polarization, with configurations using ion‑exchange membranes and porous separators to enhance selectivity and flux <cite id="5fa029ef-2">Shock ED can continuously remove radionuclides by leveraging polarization, with cells comprising ion‑exchange membranes and porous separators</cite>.

Electrodialysis is also considered promising for small‑scale, portable desalination and for high‑salinity or brine streams where RO suffers from scaling and energy penalties; recent industrial demonstrations include low‑energy seawater desalination via combined ED and continuous EDI <cite id="d311a19b-4">Due to lower capital costs and scalability, ED or ICP technologies are market‑opportunistic for small/portable desalination and for high‑salinity streams; Siemens combined ED and continuous EDI for low‑energy seawater desalination in 2011</cite>. In nutrient‑rich wastewaters, ED has been reported to remove nitrogen and phosphorus effectively, with performance linked to feed composition, pH, and membrane transport properties <cite id="5fa029ef-3">Electrodialysis performance for nutrient recovery depends on factors such as feed composition and membrane characteristics; operating challenges and costs are synthesized</cite>.

# Materials and Stack Innovations

Membrane and resin materials strongly influence salt rejection, water/ionic flux, and energy. Recent work immobilizes ion‑exchange resin particles in ionomer‑binder “wafers” that raise ionic conductivity 3–5× over non‑ionic PE binders, increasing desalination rate and lowering energy at dilute salt; water‑splitting in such wafers confirms that reducing ohmic resistances in dilute regimes yields energy savings <cite id="d311a19b-0">Ionomer‑binder resin wafers increased ionic conductivity 3–5× over PE‑binder wafers, boosting desalination rate and reducing energy; water‑splitting measurements showed resistances curtailed at dilute salt</cite>. Crosslinked anion‑exchange membranes tailored for complex ionic mixtures can achieve current efficiencies near 26% in demineralization of food solutions with ~14.9 Wh per test, illustrating how membrane chemistry and stack geometry govern measured CE and energy <cite id="faf97161-0">Hierarchical anion‑exchange membranes delivered 26.36 ± 1.79% average current efficiency and ~14.90 ± 0.30 Wh energy per test; geometry and ion migration into rinse channels affect measured CE</cite>.

At the transport level, limiting current models incorporate membrane counterion transport number tM and solution transport number tS, highlighting that membrane selectivity and conductivity set a ceiling on charge transfer without scaling/polarization interference; this motivates research on nanocomposites and higher‑conductivity matrices to push LCD and improve current efficiency at given fluxes <cite id="faf97161-4">LCD expressions include effective counterion transport numbers in membrane and solution, diffusion coefficient, and Faraday’s constant, underscoring the role of membrane/solution transport properties</cite>. EDI stacks benefit from reduced series resistance when cell pairs are minimized for a given separation target, reinforcing the design principle that fewer pairs can raise CE even as total flow capacity drops, with hydrodynamic optimization mitigating concentration polarization <cite id="faf97161-3">Fewer cell pairs yielded higher current efficiency (~16–17%) at >95% separation; CE losses are tied to membrane selectivity changes, leakage, and polarization</cite>.

# Limitations, Fouling, and Mitigation Strategies

Fouling and scaling remain central limitations. Exceeding LCD causes polarization and pH swings that precipitate metal hydroxides on membranes, reducing removal and CE; operating pH windows that avoid precipitation and using hydrodynamic regimes that suppress boundary‑layer buildup are essential <cite id="faf97161-3">Exceeding limiting current density increases resistance, causes rapid pH changes, and leads to metal hydroxide deposition and scaling; membrane pH windows are small, and damage lowers removal and current efficiency</cite>. Selectivity degradation with increasing external salt concentration raises diffusion leakage, while electroosmosis transports water proportionally to ionic current, both lowering CE unless membrane chemistry and charge regulation are tuned to feed composition <cite id="faf97161-3">Selectivity depends on external salt concentration; water transport by electroosmosis is proportional to salt transported and current; leakage, osmosis, and electroosmosis reduce current efficiency</cite>.

Current density and stack design trade‑offs also impact cost. Energy costs scale with current density, while investment costs decline with more compact stacks; an optimal current density minimizes lifecycle cost, and measured CE varies with cell‑pair count and duty cycle, guiding configuration choices in wastewater and industrial applications <cite id="faf97161-3">Energy costs increase linearly with current density while investment costs decrease; an optimal current density balances total cost; CE decreased with more cell pairs and longer operation</cite>. Pulsed electric fields and hydrodynamic features like electroconvective vortices are being explored to enhance mass transfer at manageable energy overheads, mitigating concentration polarization and potentially extending stable operating windows near LCD <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Pulsed electric fields and electroconvective vortices are discussed to enhance mass transfer and address limiting current density and polarization</cite>.

# Comparisons and Hybridization with Other Processes

Relative to RO, ED/EDI typically operate at lower specific energy for low‑to‑moderate salinity and offer modularity and minimal scaling risk in concentrate streams, but RO achieves lower specific energy at scale for very dilute brackish/sea water; ED is often favored in small‑scale or high‑salinity/brine scenarios and as a polishing stage <cite id="d311a19b-2">ED is well‑suited for low‑salinity feeds (<1700 µS/cm) and is less developed than NF/RO; RO and ED can be compared in terms of energy consumption and suitability</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-4">ED/ICP offer lower capital costs and scalability for small/portable units and high‑salinity streams; Siemens combined ED with continuous EDI for low‑energy seawater treatment</cite>. EDI’s water purity (often <0.0625 µS·cm⁻¹) is generally unattainable by RO alone without multi‑pass and lower recovery, increasing energy and brine generation; thus EDI downstream of RO is a common hybrid path in power and industrial sectors <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI achieves sub‑µS conductivity unattainable by two‑pass RO, and is used to complete desalination and polishing</cite>. In contrast to EDI, capacitive deionization (CDI) can reach 78–92% desalination below electrolysis voltages but lacks EDI’s ability to deliver 6‑digit purity; EDI remains the industrial choice for <10 µS resistivity, with specific energy often 0.39–2.11 kWh/m³ depending on configuration and duty <cite id="d311a19b-1">EDI commonly exhibits 0.39–2.11 kWh/m³ specific energy and 99.9999% desalination; CDI achieves 78–92% desalination but cannot approach EDI’s purity</cite>.

# Practical Implementation and Future Directions

Industry‑proven ED/EDI systems integrate with UF/RO to control SDI, remove dissolved ions, and meet stringent resistivity limits for boiler feed and electronics manufacturing, reducing chemical handling and producing consistent quality <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI replaces mixed beds in centralized plants, avoiding chemical regeneration burdens; it is essential for sub‑16 MΩ·cm polishing after RO</cite>. Emerging directions include ionomer‑binder resin matrices to cut series resistance, bioinspired and advanced anion‑exchange membranes to raise current efficiency, and shock ED for targeted ion capture; market trends indicate growth and sustainability‑driven integrations such as ED with filtration membranes and pulsed‑field operation to extend limits for high‑salinity and specialty feeds <cite id="d311a19b-0">Ionomer‑binder resin wafers cut resistance and energy, enabling higher desalination rates</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Bioinspired membranes and ED with filtration, pulsed fields, and shock ED are discussed for sustainable strategies</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-2">Shock ED provides efficient and selective removal of radionuclides via polarization</cite>. For decentralized PV‑powered brackish groundwater treatment, ED/EDI are evaluated alongside RO/CDI; ED is often an attractive option when salinity is low and portability and chemical minimization are priorities, with energy consumption sensitive to renewable intermittency and storage strategies <cite id="d311a19b-2">ED is an energy‑efficient option for brackish water; ED suited to low‑salinity feeds; PV energy can supply decentralized ED/RO systems, with reported thermal and electrical SECs for related electrothermal processes</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- ED/EDI remove dissolved ions via electric fields and ion‑exchange membranes/resins, achieving high salt removal, with EDI often delivering 99.9999% desalination and resistivity >17 MΩ·cm for final polishing <cite id="d311a19b-1">EDI desalination efficiency can reach 99.9999% with resistivity >17 MΩ·cm</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI completes polishing and replaces mixed beds</cite>. 
- Performance is governed by transport numbers and LCD; CE is sensitive to stack design, hydrodynamics, and pH/ionic composition, with fouling/scaling emerging when operating near LCD <cite id="faf97161-4">LCD depends on counterion transport numbers and diffusion; CE depends on selectivity and electroosmosis</cite> <cite id="faf97161-3">Exceeding LCD causes polarization and scaling; CE drops with cell‑pair number and operation time</cite>.
- Reported specific energy for ED/EDI spans ~0.39–2.11 kWh/m³ (EDI) in industrial contexts, outperforming two‑pass RO for sub‑µS targets; ED is increasingly applied for small/portable and high‑salinity scenarios and as a polishing stage in circular‑economy water systems <cite id="d311a19b-1">EDI specific energy 0.39–2.11 kWh/m³ and 99.9999% desalination</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-4">ED/ICP suitable for small/portable and high‑salinity applications; ED+EDI hybrid demonstrated low‑energy seawater treatment</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Market and sustainable‑strategy integration of ED with filtration, pulsed fields, and shock ED</cite>.
- Materials innovations (ionomer‑binder resin wafers, advanced AEMs) reduce resistance and improve CE; configuration optimization (fewer cell pairs, hydrodynamics, pulsed fields) raises CE, while fouling/scaling mitigation remains central to reliability and cost <cite id="d311a19b-0">Ionomer binder wafers raise conductivity 3–5× and reduce energy</cite> <cite id="faf97161-0">AEMs achieved ~26% CE with ~14.9 Wh per test, sensitive to geometry and migration</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Electroconvective vortices and pulsed fields enhance mass transfer, addressing LCD and polarization</cite>.

These trends suggest ED/EDI will continue to expand in niche and hybrid applications—polishing after RO, specialty ion removal, and decentralized low‑salinity treatment—where energy intensity, chemical minimization, and stringent purity drive technology choice, with materials and stack design innovations lowering barriers for broader deployment <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI downstream of RO to meet stringent limits and avoid chemical regeneration</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-3">Electrodialysis for nutrient recovery with quantified factors, challenges, and costs</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-2">ED suited to brackish groundwater; renewable PV integration enables decentralized treatment with quantified energy use</cite>.

Snippet: While electrodialysis (ED) has undergone comprehensive research and widespread application in water desalination, innovative electrochemical systems with distinctive functionalities and operational principles have emerged in recent years. Newman and Thomas-Alyea (2012) provided an overview of the development of these technologies. This laid the groundwork for the burgeoning domain of electrochemical systems dedicated to ion separation and water purification [52]. Additionally, microfluidic technologies driven by electrical energy were briefly discussed. However, their suitability for large-scale applications is limited compared to electrochemical systems, which offer clear pathways for scale-up through components such as electrodes, porous separators, and ion exchange membranes, which can be manufactured in substantial areas.

Title: Advancing electrodeionization with conductive ionomer binders that immobilize ion-exchange resin particles into porous wafer substrates
Snippet: Electrodeionization (EDI) is an electrically driven separations technology that employs ion-exchange membranes and resin particles. Deionization occurs under the influence of an applied electric field, facilitating continuous regeneration of the resins and supplementing ionic conductivity. While EDI is commercially used for ultrapure water production, material innovation is required for improving desalination performance and energy efficiency for treating alternative water supplies. This work reports a new class of ion-exchange resin-wafers (RWs) fabricated with ion-conductive binders that exhibit exceptional ionic conductivities—a 3–5-fold improvement over conventional RWs that contain a non-ionic polyethylene binder. Incorporation into an EDI stack (RW-EDI) resulted in an increased desalination rate and reduced energy expenditure compared to the conventional RWs. The water-splitting phenomenon was also investigated in the RW in an external experimental setup in this work. Overall, this work demonstrates that ohmic resistances can be substantially curtailed with ionomer binder RWs at dilute salt concentrations.
</snippet>

Snippet: The most important case study was carried out on the make-up water for boilers. This water represents the highest standards of quality and strict limits of conductivity, concentration of ions, suspended and colloidal solids and dissolved gasses, as determined by national or European standards (in the European Union) [12]. The conductivity of make-up water for high-pressure boilers should be as close as possible to theoretical water (i.e., clear water containing just H 2 O) exhibiting a resistivity of more than 17 MΩ cm −1 . The arrangement of membrane units in the pilot test was inspired by the combination of membrane processes commonly used in western European countries. These consist of ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis and electrodeionization. The main purpose of an ultrafiltration unit is to decrease the silt density index (SDI 15 < 5) before feeding the reverse osmosis. The reverse osmosis substitutes classical ion exchange demineralization units. The downstream electrodeionization unit then completes the desalination process and polishes the water.

The technology of electrodeionization substitutes mixed beds, because it avoids the additional problems with the chemicals used in the regeneration of mixed beds (e.g., liquid wastes, neutralization of wastes), administration, the transportation of chemicals and wastes, large built-up area, semi-automatic operation, etc. Electrodeionization (EDI) is intended for polishing the reverse osmosis (RO) permeate. It is an essential process which cannot be simply substituted by two-pass (or more) reverse osmosis. The two-pass reverse osmosis usually serves for sequential decarbonization and desilication. The conductivity of the osmosis permeate from the second pass is approximately 1 µS cm −1 . The energy consumption of two-pass reverse osmosis is higher in comparison with electrodeionization, and the recovery rate is also lower. Two-pass reverse osmosis is used when the hardness of raw water is too high, or when we want to achieve a water quality after electrodeionization that is better than 16 MΩ cm −1 (<0.0625 µS cm −1 ). The energy costs increase linearly as the current density increases, whereas the investment costs decrease. Therefore, there is a value of the current density that optimizes the total cost. Measuring the current efficiency under different experimental conditions, we found that the current efficiency decreased with increases in the number of cell pairs and operating time. However, in the case of 5 pairs and 9 pairs, the current efficiency was approximately 16% and 17%, respectively, when the efficiency of heavy metals separation exceeded 95% (Fig. 6). Therefore, the fewer the cell pairs, the higher the efficiency of the current, because the ion separation performance decreases at each incremental step (pair). Thus, the efficiency of the current is a measure of the electric power used for ion separation. 

The loss of current efficiency is largely determined by the selectivity of the membrane and its scaling, e.g. in water movement, current leakage, and failing because of osmosis and electroosmosis. The selectivity of the ion-selective membrane strongly depends on the concentration of salt in the external solution. When this increases, the intensity of the diffusion flux from the external solution into the membrane increases. The amount of water transported Fig. 6. Generally, exceeding the LCD causes concentration polarization at the surface of the ion exchange membrane [2,32]. In electrodialysis, exceeding the LCD results in the electrical resistance of the solution increasing, leading to a drastic drop in the efficiency of the process. Additionally, the dissolution of water can cause a rapid change in pH in the solution on the ion exchange membrane surface. This change in pH can lead to the deposition of metal hydroxides at the surface of the ion exchange membrane, resulting in scaling [8]. If the range of the operating pH of the membrane is small, the membrane may be damaged, resulting in lower removal and current efficiency [2].

# Overview: What Electrodialysis Is and Why It Matters

Electrodialysis (ED) is an electrically driven membrane separation process that uses ion‑exchange membranes (anion‑ and cation‑selective) arranged in stacks to remove dissolved salts and other ions from water by transporting them toward oppositely charged electrodes under an applied electric field, concentrating them in specific compartments while desalinating the “diluate” streams <cite id="5fa029ef-0">Electrodialysis is one of the common membrane technologies used for water desalination, with advantages, limitations, and challenges discussed in a recent review</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Electrodialytic systems comprise ion exchange membranes and associated phenomena; recent developments include electroconvection, pulsed fields, electrodeionization, and shock electrodialysis</cite>. ED is commercially deployed, with market activity spanning decades and a growing pipeline of sustainable strategies and circular‑economy applications <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Market overviews show global revenues, manufacturers, and trends, linking electrodialytic phenomena to sustainable strategies and eco‑efficient integrations</cite>.

Electrodeionization (EDI) extends ED by integrating ion‑exchange resins and membranes in flow channels with applied electric fields to continuously regenerate resins and drive ion transport, producing ultrapure water often used as polishing after reverse osmosis (RO) or as a standalone deionization unit <cite id="d311a19b-0">EDI employs ion‑exchange membranes and resin particles under an applied electric field, enabling continuous regeneration and conductivity supplementation for ultrapure water production</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI substitutes mixed‑bed ion exchange in boiler makeup treatment and is essential for polishing RO permeate to resistivity >17 MΩ·cm</cite>. Shock electrodialysis (shock ED) is an emerging variant that leverages electric fields and ion concentration polarization to concentrate and remove specific ions, including radionuclides, with recent demonstrations using ion‑exchange membranes and porous separators <cite id="5fa029ef-2">Shock electrodialysis induces ion transport and separation via polarization to remove radionuclides; earlier work proposed its suitability over traditional precipitation/adsorption, using ion‑exchange membranes and porous separators</cite>.

# Device Configuration and Operating Modes

In ED stacks, alternating anion‑ and cation‑exchange membranes form selective compartments where cations and anions migrate toward cathode/ anode, respectively, into concentrate channels; diluate channels thereby lose ions and are desalinated <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Principles and state‑of‑the‑art membrane phenomena, including limiting current density, electroconvective vortices, and pulsed fields, are associated with ED stacks and transport equations</cite>. Operation can be direct current (DC) or pulsed/alternating fields; pulsed fields can enhance mass transfer and mitigate concentration polarization, with electroconvective vortices aiding transport near membranes <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Electroconvective vortices and pulsed‑electric fields are discussed as mechanisms to enhance mass transfer in electrodialytic systems</cite>.

EDI integrates flow‑through ion‑exchange resins between membrane pairs in channels; applied potential drives ions from feed/leach streams into adjacent concentrate compartments while resins are continuously regenerated electrochemically, reducing chemical regeneration needs compared to mixed beds <cite id="d311a19b-0">EDI continuously regenerates resins and supplements conductivity, enabling ultrapure water production</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI downstream of RO/polishing to ultra‑low conductivity; replaces mixed beds due to avoidance of chemical regeneration issues and complex operations</cite>. Current research also explores shock ED cells and hybrid ED‑filtration integrations for sustainability and performance tailoring <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Applications include shock electrodialysis and ED with filtration membranes, with sustainable strategies proposed for circular economy contexts</cite>.

# Transport Concepts: Current Efficiency, Limiting Current, and Selectivity

Current efficiency (CE) quantifies the fraction of applied charge used to transport target ions; it is commonly computed from measured current and ion transfer equivalents using Faraday’s constant and stack geometry, and is central to assessing energy use and applicability <cite id="faf97161-1">Current utilization (current efficiency, Coulombic/charge efficiency) is the ratio of current used to effectively separate salt ions to total applied current, typically >90% in desalination processes</cite> <cite id="faf97161-2">CE compares moles of ion transferred to Faradays consumed; it indicates how effectively ions are transported per applied current</cite>. CE depends strongly on membrane selectivity, pH, and hydrodynamics; scaling and hydroxide deposition at membranes, leakage via electroosmosis, and transport through membrane “leakage” channels all reduce CE and ion removal <cite id="faf97161-3">Current efficiency decreases with more cell pairs and longer operation; fewer cell pairs give higher current efficiency when metal removal >95%; losses arise from membrane selectivity changes, scaling, leakage, and osmosis/electroosmosis; exceeding limiting current density causes polarization and rapid pH swings leading to hydroxide scaling</cite>.

The limiting current density (LCD) is set by diffusion‑controlled transport of counterions from feed to concentrate streams; simple models such as the Lévêque approximation express LCD in terms of ion valence, bulk concentration, membrane and solution transport numbers, diffusion coefficient, and membrane conductivity <cite id="faf97161-4">Theoretical LCD can be calculated with Lévêque equations using counterion charge, concentration, effective transport numbers in membrane and solution, diffusion coefficient, and Faraday’s constant</cite>. Exceeding LCD accelerates polarization, pH swings, and scaling, reducing efficiency and membrane lifetime unless mitigated by hydrodynamics, pH buffering, or bipolar membranes to route non‑target ions to alternate streams <cite id="faf97161-3">Exceeding LCD increases solution electrical resistance, drops process efficiency, and induces rapid pH changes that cause hydroxide deposition and scaling</cite>.

# Performance Metrics and Benchmarks

Energy consumption is typically reported as specific electrical energy (kWh/m³) or normalized by salinity and current density. For ED/EDI systems treating brackish groundwater or low‑salinity streams, reported specific energy consumption spans roughly 0.39–2.11 kWh/m³ for EDI in power‑sector case studies, with ED often lower depending on stack/membrane/resin design and duty cycle <cite id="d311a19b-1">Specific energy consumption of EDI commonly ranges from 0.39 to 2.11 kW·m⁻³; EDI’s use of membranes and resins lowers resistance of deeply deionized water relative to electrochemical competitors</cite>. EDI can achieve near‑complete desalination (99.9999%) to produce water with resistivity >17 MΩ·cm, whereas two‑pass RO struggles to reach comparable purity and requires more energy and lower recovery; EDI is often unavoidable to reach <0.0625 µS·cm⁻¹ conductivity targets <cite id="d311a19b-1">Theoretical and practical EDI desalination efficiency can reach 99.9999%, producing water with resistivity exceeding 17 MΩ·cm, outperforming two‑pass RO in both quality and energy recovery for sub‑16 MΩ·cm targets</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI completes polishing after RO and avoids chemical regeneration complexities; two‑pass RO is not cost‑effective for producing water better than 16 MΩ·cm</cite>.

Measured current efficiencies vary by configuration and ion. In a food‑solution demineralization stack, an averaged current efficiency of ~26% was achieved using potassium as the tracer, with energy consumption ~14.9 Wh per test; lower values than literature were attributed to migration into a rinse stream and geometry, underscoring the sensitivity of CE to stack design and measurement boundaries <cite id="faf97161-0">Averaged current efficiency of 26.36 ± 1.79% and energy consumption ~14.90 ± 0.30 Wh were observed; lower efficiencies than prior hCEM work were linked to cation migration into a rinse compartment and stack geometry</cite>. In heavy‑metal‑containing wastewater, current efficiency around 16–17% at >95% separation was observed for 5–9 cell‑pair stacks, declining with more pairs and longer operation, highlighting a trade‑off between throughput and charge usage and the need to optimize current density and hydrodynamics to minimize cost <cite id="faf97161-3">Current efficiency decreased with cell‑pair number and operating time; with 5–9 pairs, CE ~16–17% coincided with >95% separation; fewer pairs improved current efficiency due to reduced stepwise performance loss</cite>.

# Applications Across Water Treatment and Resource Recovery

Electrodialytic processes are widely applied in desalination and demineralization for power sector makeup, industrial process water, and alternatives to mixed‑bed demineralizers, achieving stringent conductivity targets that exceed RO permeate alone <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI integrates after UF/RO to meet stringent boiler makeup limits; it completes softening and heavy metal removal and cannot be simply substituted by two‑pass RO</cite>. EDI’s continuous electrochemical regeneration of resins has made it a commercial mainstay for ultrapure water, with documented replacement of mixed beds in centralized plants <cite id="d311a19b-0">EDI is commercially used for ultrapure water; resin immobilization in ionomer‑binder wafers improved desalination rates and reduced energy at dilute salt concentrations</cite>.

Beyond drinking water, ED/EDI are used for nutrient recovery from wastewater, where systematic studies quantify how operating factors and membrane choices affect electrodialytic efficiency and cost, providing decision frameworks for designers and policymakers <cite id="5fa029ef-3">A systematic review classifies essential factors affecting ED efficiency in nutrient recovery and discusses operating challenges and costs</cite>. In specialty applications, ED variants like shock ED have demonstrated continuous removal of radionuclides by exploiting ion concentration polarization, with configurations using ion‑exchange membranes and porous separators to enhance selectivity and flux <cite id="5fa029ef-2">Shock ED can continuously remove radionuclides by leveraging polarization, with cells comprising ion‑exchange membranes and porous separators</cite>.

Electrodialysis is also considered promising for small‑scale, portable desalination and for high‑salinity or brine streams where RO suffers from scaling and energy penalties; recent industrial demonstrations include low‑energy seawater desalination via combined ED and continuous EDI <cite id="d311a19b-4">Due to lower capital costs and scalability, ED or ICP technologies are market‑opportunistic for small/portable desalination and for high‑salinity streams; Siemens combined ED and continuous EDI for low‑energy seawater desalination in 2011</cite>. In nutrient‑rich wastewaters, ED has been reported to remove nitrogen and phosphorus effectively, with performance linked to feed composition, pH, and membrane transport properties <cite id="5fa029ef-3">Electrodialysis performance for nutrient recovery depends on factors such as feed composition and membrane characteristics; operating challenges and costs are synthesized</cite>.

# Materials and Stack Innovations

Membrane and resin materials strongly influence salt rejection, water/ionic flux, and energy. Recent work immobilizes ion‑exchange resin particles in ionomer‑binder “wafers” that raise ionic conductivity 3–5× over non‑ionic PE binders, increasing desalination rate and lowering energy at dilute salt; water‑splitting in such wafers confirms that reducing ohmic resistances in dilute regimes yields energy savings <cite id="d311a19b-0">Ionomer‑binder resin wafers increased ionic conductivity 3–5× over PE‑binder wafers, boosting desalination rate and reducing energy; water‑splitting measurements showed resistances curtailed at dilute salt</cite>. Crosslinked anion‑exchange membranes tailored for complex ionic mixtures can achieve current efficiencies near 26% in demineralization of food solutions with ~14.9 Wh per test, illustrating how membrane chemistry and stack geometry govern measured CE and energy <cite id="faf97161-0">Hierarchical anion‑exchange membranes delivered 26.36 ± 1.79% average current efficiency and ~14.90 ± 0.30 Wh energy per test; geometry and ion migration into rinse channels affect measured CE</cite>.

At the transport level, limiting current models incorporate membrane counterion transport number tM and solution transport number tS, highlighting that membrane selectivity and conductivity set a ceiling on charge transfer without scaling/polarization interference; this motivates research on nanocomposites and higher‑conductivity matrices to push LCD and improve current efficiency at given fluxes <cite id="faf97161-4">LCD expressions include effective counterion transport numbers in membrane and solution, diffusion coefficient, and Faraday’s constant, underscoring the role of membrane/solution transport properties</cite>. EDI stacks benefit from reduced series resistance when cell pairs are minimized for a given separation target, reinforcing the design principle that fewer pairs can raise CE even as total flow capacity drops, with hydrodynamic optimization mitigating concentration polarization <cite id="faf97161-3">Fewer cell pairs yielded higher current efficiency (~16–17%) at >95% separation; CE losses are tied to membrane selectivity changes, leakage, and polarization</cite>.

# Limitations, Fouling, and Mitigation Strategies

Fouling and scaling remain central limitations. Exceeding LCD causes polarization and pH swings that precipitate metal hydroxides on membranes, reducing removal and CE; operating pH windows that avoid precipitation and using hydrodynamic regimes that suppress boundary‑layer buildup are essential <cite id="faf97161-3">Exceeding limiting current density increases resistance, causes rapid pH changes, and leads to metal hydroxide deposition and scaling; membrane pH windows are small, and damage lowers removal and current efficiency</cite>. Selectivity degradation with increasing external salt concentration raises diffusion leakage, while electroosmosis transports water proportionally to ionic current, both lowering CE unless membrane chemistry and charge regulation are tuned to feed composition <cite id="faf97161-3">Selectivity depends on external salt concentration; water transport by electroosmosis is proportional to salt transported and current; leakage, osmosis, and electroosmosis reduce current efficiency</cite>.

Current density and stack design trade‑offs also impact cost. Energy costs scale with current density, while investment costs decline with more compact stacks; an optimal current density minimizes lifecycle cost, and measured CE varies with cell‑pair count and duty cycle, guiding configuration choices in wastewater and industrial applications <cite id="faf97161-3">Energy costs increase linearly with current density while investment costs decrease; an optimal current density balances total cost; CE decreased with more cell pairs and longer operation</cite>. Pulsed electric fields and hydrodynamic features like electroconvective vortices are being explored to enhance mass transfer at manageable energy overheads, mitigating concentration polarization and potentially extending stable operating windows near LCD <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Pulsed electric fields and electroconvective vortices are discussed to enhance mass transfer and address limiting current density and polarization</cite>.

# Comparisons and Hybridization with Other Processes

Relative to RO, ED/EDI typically operate at lower specific energy for low‑to‑moderate salinity and offer modularity and minimal scaling risk in concentrate streams, but RO achieves lower specific energy at scale for very dilute brackish/sea water; ED is often favored in small‑scale or high‑salinity/brine scenarios and as a polishing stage <cite id="d311a19b-2">ED is well‑suited for low‑salinity feeds (<1700 µS/cm) and is less developed than NF/RO; RO and ED can be compared in terms of energy consumption and suitability</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-4">ED/ICP offer lower capital costs and scalability for small/portable units and high‑salinity streams; Siemens combined ED with continuous EDI for low‑energy seawater treatment</cite>. EDI’s water purity (often <0.0625 µS·cm⁻¹) is generally unattainable by RO alone without multi‑pass and lower recovery, increasing energy and brine generation; thus EDI downstream of RO is a common hybrid path in power and industrial sectors <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI achieves sub‑µS conductivity unattainable by two‑pass RO, and is used to complete desalination and polishing</cite>. In contrast to EDI, capacitive deionization (CDI) can reach 78–92% desalination below electrolysis voltages but lacks EDI’s ability to deliver 6‑digit purity; EDI remains the industrial choice for <10 µS resistivity, with specific energy often 0.39–2.11 kWh/m³ depending on configuration and duty <cite id="d311a19b-1">EDI commonly exhibits 0.39–2.11 kWh/m³ specific energy and 99.9999% desalination; CDI achieves 78–92% desalination but cannot approach EDI’s purity</cite>.

# Practical Implementation and Future Directions

Industry‑proven ED/EDI systems integrate with UF/RO to control SDI, remove dissolved ions, and meet stringent resistivity limits for boiler feed and electronics manufacturing, reducing chemical handling and producing consistent quality <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI replaces mixed beds in centralized plants, avoiding chemical regeneration burdens; it is essential for sub‑16 MΩ·cm polishing after RO</cite>. Emerging directions include ionomer‑binder resin matrices to cut series resistance, bioinspired and advanced anion‑exchange membranes to raise current efficiency, and shock ED for targeted ion capture; market trends indicate growth and sustainability‑driven integrations such as ED with filtration membranes and pulsed‑field operation to extend limits for high‑salinity and specialty feeds <cite id="d311a19b-0">Ionomer‑binder resin wafers cut resistance and energy, enabling higher desalination rates</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Bioinspired membranes and ED with filtration, pulsed fields, and shock ED are discussed for sustainable strategies</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-2">Shock ED provides efficient and selective removal of radionuclides via polarization</cite>. For decentralized PV‑powered brackish groundwater treatment, ED/EDI are evaluated alongside RO/CDI; ED is often an attractive option when salinity is low and portability and chemical minimization are priorities, with energy consumption sensitive to renewable intermittency and storage strategies <cite id="d311a19b-2">ED is an energy‑efficient option for brackish water; ED suited to low‑salinity feeds; PV energy can supply decentralized ED/RO systems, with reported thermal and electrical SECs for related electrothermal processes</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- ED/EDI remove dissolved ions via electric fields and ion‑exchange membranes/resins, achieving high salt removal, with EDI often delivering 99.9999% desalination and resistivity >17 MΩ·cm for final polishing <cite id="d311a19b-1">EDI desalination efficiency can reach 99.9999% with resistivity >17 MΩ·cm</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI completes polishing and replaces mixed beds</cite>. 
- Performance is governed by transport numbers and LCD; CE is sensitive to stack design, hydrodynamics, and pH/ionic composition, with fouling/scaling emerging when operating near LCD <cite id="faf97161-4">LCD depends on counterion transport numbers and diffusion; CE depends on selectivity and electroosmosis</cite> <cite id="faf97161-3">Exceeding LCD causes polarization and scaling; CE drops with cell‑pair number and operation time</cite>.
- Reported specific energy for ED/EDI spans ~0.39–2.11 kWh/m³ (EDI) in industrial contexts, outperforming two‑pass RO for sub‑µS targets; ED is increasingly applied for small/portable and high‑salinity scenarios and as a polishing stage in circular‑economy water systems <cite id="d311a19b-1">EDI specific energy 0.39–2.11 kWh/m³ and 99.9999% desalination</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-4">ED/ICP suitable for small/portable and high‑salinity applications; ED+EDI hybrid demonstrated low‑energy seawater treatment</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Market and sustainable‑strategy integration of ED with filtration, pulsed fields, and shock ED</cite>.
- Materials innovations (ionomer‑binder resin wafers, advanced AEMs) reduce resistance and improve CE; configuration optimization (fewer cell pairs, hydrodynamics, pulsed fields) raises CE, while fouling/scaling mitigation remains central to reliability and cost <cite id="d311a19b-0">Ionomer binder wafers raise conductivity 3–5× and reduce energy</cite> <cite id="faf97161-0">AEMs achieved ~26% CE with ~14.9 Wh per test, sensitive to geometry and migration</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-1">Electroconvective vortices and pulsed fields enhance mass transfer, addressing LCD and polarization</cite>.

These trends suggest ED/EDI will continue to expand in niche and hybrid applications—polishing after RO, specialty ion removal, and decentralized low‑salinity treatment—where energy intensity, chemical minimization, and stringent purity drive technology choice, with materials and stack design innovations lowering barriers for broader deployment <cite id="d311a19b-3">EDI downstream of RO to meet stringent limits and avoid chemical regeneration</cite> <cite id="5fa029ef-3">Electrodialysis for nutrient recovery with quantified factors, challenges, and costs</cite> <cite id="d311a19b-2">ED suited to brackish groundwater; renewable PV integration enables decentralized treatment with quantified energy use</cite>.

Title: ELECTRODIALYSIS (ED): A REVIEW ON THE FUNDAMENTAL CONCEPT, ADVANTAGES, LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE TREND
Snippet: The membrane-based method is one of the most widely applied and commercially proven desalination technologies in recent years. Electrodialysis (ED) is one of the common membrane technologies used for water desalination. This review paper aims to provide the fundamental concept of electrodialysis and its application in water desalination. The advantages, limitations, challenges, and future trends of electrodialysis have been discussed and delineated.Keywords: electrodialysis, reversal, fouling, membranes

Title: Electrodialytic Processes: Market Overview, Membrane Phenomena, Recent Developments and Sustainable Strategies
Snippet: 9][10][11], but rather to give a global portrait of the most recent developments in electrodialytic membrane phenomena and their uses or potential uses in sustainable strategies or in a circular economy. For this purpose, the authors mainly focused on articles reported in the literature from 2015 to June 2020. The review starts with an overview of the electrodialytic system market, including the global revenues, the main system manufacturers and their evolution in terms of number during the last 50 years. Then, the principles and state of the art on membrane phenomena, limiting current density, electroconvective vortices and pulsed electric field are described and the main equations associated to mass transfer are shortly presented. After that, the most recent developments based on electrodialytic membrane phenomena such as applications of electroconvective vortices, use of pulsed-electric field, electrodeionization and shock electrodialysis are discussed. Based on these new developments or technologies, the integration of electrodialytic technologies in sustainable strategies or use of eco-efficient new electrodialytic technologies such as electrodialysis with filtration membrane are presented and proposed.

Title: State-of-the-Art Review on Removal of Naturally Occurring Radioactive Materials in Water
Snippet: While electrodialysis (ED) has undergone comprehensive research and widespread application in water desalination, innovative electrochemical systems with distinctive functionalities and operational principles have emerged in recent years. These include shock electrodialysis (shock ED), electrodeionization (EDI), capacitive deionization (CDI), and Faradaic electrosorption. Newman and Thomas-Alyea (2012) provided an overview of the development of these technologies. This laid the groundwork for the burgeoning domain of electrochemical systems dedicated to ion separation and water purification [52]. Additionally, microfluidic technologies driven by electrical energy were briefly discussed. However, their suitability for large-scale applications is limited compared to electrochemical systems, which offer clear pathways for scale-up through components such as electrodes, porous separators, and ion exchange membranes, which can be manufactured in substantial areas. 

In an earlier study, Alkhadra et al. (2019) [40] explored the application of shock electrodialysis to continuously remove radionuclides from contaminated water [42]. Traditional methods for radionuclide removal, such as precipitation and adsorption, often require high removal efficiency and have many operational limitations. Alkhadra et al. (2019) [40] proposed that shock electrodialysis can effectively address these challenges. Shock electrodialysis is an emerging electrochemical method that uses electric fields to induce ion transport and separation in water [40]. This technique leverages the principle of ion concentration polarization to achieve the efficient and selective removal of radionuclides. In the study, the researchers designed and fabricated a shock electrodialysis cell consisting of an ion exchange membrane and a porous separator.

Title: Advancing electrodeionization with conductive ionomer binders that immobilize ion-exchange resin particles into porous wafer substrates
Snippet: Electrodeionization (EDI) is an electrically driven separations technology that employs ion-exchange membranes and resin particles. Deionization occurs under the influence of an applied electric field, facilitating continuous regeneration of the resins and supplementing ionic conductivity. While EDI is commercially used for ultrapure water production, material innovation is required for improving desalination performance and energy efficiency for treating alternative water supplies. This work reports a new class of ion-exchange resin-wafers (RWs) fabricated with ion-conductive binders that exhibit exceptional ionic conductivities—a 3–5-fold improvement over conventional RWs that contain a non-ionic polyethylene binder. Incorporation into an EDI stack (RW-EDI) resulted in an increased desalination rate and reduced energy expenditure compared to the conventional RWs. The water-splitting phenomenon was also investigated in the RW in an external experimental setup in this work. Overall, this work demonstrates that ohmic resistances can be substantially curtailed with ionomer binder RWs at dilute salt concentrations.

Title: State-of-the-Art Water Treatment in Czech Power Sector: Industry-Proven Case Studies Showing Economic and Technical Benefits of Membrane and Other Novel Technologies for Each Particular Water Cycle
Snippet: The most important case study was carried out on the make-up water for boilers. This water represents the highest standards of quality and strict limits of conductivity, concentration of ions, suspended and colloidal solids and dissolved gasses, as determined by national or European standards (in the European Union) [12]. The conductivity of make-up water for high-pressure boilers should be as close as possible to theoretical water (i.e., clear water containing just H 2 O) exhibiting a resistivity of more than 17 MΩ cm −1 . The arrangement of membrane units in the pilot test was inspired by the combination of membrane processes commonly used in western European countries. These consist of ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis and electrodeionization. The main purpose of an ultrafiltration unit is to decrease the silt density index (SDI 15 < 5) before feeding the reverse osmosis. The reverse osmosis substitutes classical ion exchange demineralization units. The downstream electrodeionization unit then completes the desalination process and polishes the water.

The technology of electrodeionization substitutes mixed beds, because it avoids the additional problems with the chemicals used in the regeneration of mixed beds (e.g., liquid wastes, neutralization of wastes), administration, the transportation of chemicals and wastes, large built-up area, semi-automatic operation, etc. Electrodeionization (EDI) is intended for polishing the reverse osmosis (RO) permeate. It is an essential process which cannot be simply substituted by two-pass (or more) reverse osmosis. The two-pass reverse osmosis usually serves for sequential decarbonization and desilication. The conductivity of the osmosis permeate from the second pass is approximately 1 µS cm −1 . The energy consumption of two-pass reverse osmosis is higher in comparison with electrodeionization, and the recovery rate is also lower. Since ED and ICP technologies are generally requiring lower capital costs, and also scalable (it can be implemented in small and medium scale systems), there is a market opportunity for ED or ICP technologies in small, portable desalination units, even for seawater. In addition, feed water with higher salinity (50 k ppm or more) than seawater is actually precipitously challenging to treat with RO, while electrochemical methods may be the most promising option 3,40 . Due to the reasons mentioned above, we believe that it is justifiable to ED/ICP technologies for the treatment of seawater or even brine. Recently, as a example to show this possibility, Siemens presents the low-energy seawater desalination by combining ED and continuous electrodeionization in 2011 43 .

documents.snippet: Electrodeionization (EDI) is an electrically driven separations technology that employs ion-exchange membranes and resin particles. Deionization occurs under the influence of an applied electric field, facilitating continuous regeneration of the resins and supplementing ionic conductivity. While EDI is commercially used for ultrapure water production, material innovation is required for improving desalination performance and energy efficiency for treating alternative water supplies. This work reports a new class of ion-exchange resin-wafers (RWs) fabricated with ion-conductive binders that exhibit exceptional ionic conductivities—a 3–5-fold improvement over conventional RWs that contain a non-ionic polyethylene binder. Incorporation into an EDI stack (RW-EDI) resulted in an increased desalination rate and reduced energy expenditure compared to the conventional RWs. The water-splitting phenomenon was also investigated in the RW in an external experimental setup in this work. Overall, this work demonstrates that ohmic resistances can be substantially curtailed with ionomer binder RWs at dilute salt concentrations.

Four main representative processes were selected as optional future methods of desalination. The first of them, capacitive deionization (CDI), could potentially replace EDI. The RO + CDI combination thus constitutes an optional system for ultrapure make-up water for boilers. The specific energy consumption of EDI commonly ranges from 0.39 to 2.11 kW m −3 , while for CDI, it is 0.02-0.22 kW m −3 . However, for each particular case the EDI consumption is lower due to the utilization of membranes and resin in between the electrodes, which together decrease the resistance of deeply deionized water [28]. Moreover, the so-far maximum desalination reached by the CDI electrochemical method, which operates below the potential of water electrolysis to avoid byproducts (theoretically 1.2 V; approx. 2.4 V for surface water or 1.4 V for permeate from pressure membrane processes), was 78-92% desalination efficiency, while EDI can provide 99.9999% desalination efficiency. This makes it a suitable process for the softening of water or heavy metal removal [13,29].

The recent trends bring about the development of electrodes in flow form [30].

The second process is forward osmosis (FO). Compared to RO, FO is successfully applied for waters with 70.000 ppm and higher salinity, and for such waters the energy consumption is 29.45-29.91 kW m −3 [13,31]. This process might therefore be used for the pretreatment of salty water (sea water) before reverse osmosis, but it still utilizes the same membranes as RO, so FO needs a pretreatment by means of UF or MF. documents.snippet:
Several challenges exist for the identification of optimum material for manufacturing electrodes [5].Other electrically driven separation desalination processes-such as electrodeionization (EDI) and electrodialysis (ED)-transport charged ions in a solution by utilizing an electric field.EDI is an energy-efficient option for brackish water desalination.Whilst ED exhibits significant promise and is well-suited for treating lower salinity feedwater (<1700 µS/cm) [6], it remains much less developed than NF/RO membrane technology.

Many remote regions of developing countries that possess a significant solar energy resource are also located far away from the coast, thus suggesting that the most energyefficient treatment option would be the desalination of brackish groundwater.For such applications, pilot-scale NF/RO membrane technology has been widely used as an energyefficient and robust option for the provision of clean drinking water [7,8].In order to make the desalination technology more sustainable, renewable energy sources are increasingly deployed for providing the energy requirements.When renewable energy-powered membrane (RE-membrane) systems are deployed in remote areas that lack an electricity grid, such decentralized technologies can provide an ideal solution.In particular, photovoltaic (PV) energy has become an affordable source of clean electricity due to steady price declines over the last decade [7] and is currently (2020 data) one of the cheapest sources of electricity [9].When examining energy efficiency and cost estimations, many of the emerging technologies are based on bench-scale systems.In addition, the majority of these technologies are typified by having a high energy consumption.Recent investigations at the Plataforma Solar de Almeria indicated that vacuum-assisted air gap MD technology could reduce the SEC [10,11].The pilot MD system for seawater desalination -which exhibited an electrical conductivity (ED) of 37-40 mS/cm -exhibited a thermal SEC of 208 kWh/m 3 and an electrical SEC of 5-20 kWh/m 3 [10].However, the water cost was hardly comparable due to the large data variations and different applications from the literature [11].

The most important case study was carried out on the make-up water for boilers. This water represents the highest standards of quality and strict limits of conductivity, concentration of ions, suspended and colloidal solids and dissolved gasses, as determined by national or European standards (in the European Union) [12]. The conductivity of make-up water for high-pressure boilers should be as close as possible to theoretical water (i.e., clear water containing just H 2 O) exhibiting a resistivity of more than 17 MΩ cm −1 . The arrangement of membrane units in the pilot test was inspired by the combination of membrane processes commonly used in western European countries. These consist of ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis and electrodeionization. The main purpose of an ultrafiltration unit is to decrease the silt density index (SDI 15 < 5) before feeding the reverse osmosis. The reverse osmosis substitutes classical ion exchange demineralization units. The downstream electrodeionization unit then completes the desalination process and polishes the water.

The technology of electrodeionization substitutes mixed beds, because it avoids the additional problems with the chemicals used in the regeneration of mixed beds (e.g., liquid wastes, neutralization of wastes), administration, the transportation of chemicals and wastes, large built-up area, semi-automatic operation, etc. Electrodeionization (EDI) is intended for polishing the reverse osmosis (RO) permeate. It is an essential process which cannot be simply substituted by two-pass (or more) reverse osmosis. The two-pass reverse osmosis usually serves for sequential decarbonization and desilication. The conductivity of the osmosis permeate from the second pass is approximately 1 µS cm −1 . The energy consumption of two-pass reverse osmosis is higher in comparison with electrodeionization, and the recovery rate is also lower. Two-pass reverse osmosis is used when the hardness of raw water is too high, or when we want to achieve a water quality after electrodeionization that is better than 16 MΩ cm −1 (<0.0625 µS cm −1 ). Therefore, the electrodeionization process is unavoidable in the preparation of the make-

Since ED and ICP technologies are generally requiring lower capital costs, and also scalable (it can be implemented in small and medium scale systems), there is a market opportunity for ED or ICP technologies in small, portable desalination units, even for seawater. In addition, feed water with higher salinity (50 k ppm or more) than seawater is actually precipitously challenging to treat with RO, while electrochemical methods may be the most promising option 3,40 . Due to the reasons mentioned above, we believe that it is justifiable to ED/ICP technologies for the treatment of seawater or even brine. The energy costs increase linearly as the current density increases, whereas the investment costs decrease. Therefore, there is a value of the current density that optimizes the total cost. Measuring the current efficiency under different experimental conditions, we found that the current efficiency decreased with increases in the number of cell pairs and operating time. However, in the case of 5 pairs and 9 pairs, the current efficiency was approximately 16% and 17%, respectively, when the efficiency of heavy metals separation exceeded 95% (Fig. 6). Therefore, the fewer the cell pairs, the higher the efficiency of the current, because the ion separation performance decreases at each incremental step (pair). Thus, the efficiency of the current is a measure of the electric power used for ion separation. 

The loss of current efficiency is largely determined by the selectivity of the membrane and its scaling, e.g. in water movement, current leakage, and failing because of osmosis and electroosmosis. The selectivity of the ion-selective membrane strongly depends on the concentration of salt in the external solution. When this increases, the intensity of the diffusion flux from the external solution into the membrane increases. The amount of water transported Fig. 6. because of electroosmosis is proportional to the amount of salt transported from the diluate to concentration cell, i.e. It is directly proportional to the electric current (charge) passing through the membranes. 

Generally, exceeding the LCD causes concentration polarization at the surface of the ion exchange membrane [2,32]. In electrodialysis, exceeding the LCD results in the electrical resistance of the solution increasing, leading to a drastic drop in the efficiency of the process. Additionally, the dissolution of water can cause a rapid change in pH in the solution on the ion exchange membrane surface. This change in pH can lead to the deposition of metal hydroxides at the surface of the ion exchange membrane, resulting in scaling [8]. If the range of the operating pH of the membrane is small, the membrane may be damaged, resulting in lower removal and current efficiency [2].

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer clearly defines electrodialysis in the first paragraph as 'an electrically driven membrane separation process that uses ion-exchange membranes (anion- and cation-selective) arranged in stacks to remove dissolved salts and other ions from water by transporting them toward oppositely charged electrodes under an applied electric field.' This definition explicitly includes all required elements: (1) it is a membrane-based separation process, (2) it uses an electric field, and (3) it transports ions through ion-exchange membranes.
