Summary answer
Electrodialysis achieves continuous ultrapure water production by using electric fields and ion‑selective membranes to drive continuous ionic transport and membrane polarization, with optional polarity reversal and over‑limiting regimes to maintain steady flow without batch stops; electrodeionization (EDI) further integrates ion‑exchange resins and membranes so that water dissociation at the diluate side electrochemically regenerates the resins continuously, eliminating the need for external acid/alkali regeneration cycles and enabling automated, hands‑off production of water with resistivity >15–18 MΩ·cm. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Continuous processes such as Electrodialysis and Filled‑Cell Electrodialysis/Continuous Electrodeionization use alternating cationic and anionic permselective membranes under an applied field to create diluate/concentrate compartments, with deionization occurring continuously as ions permeate while coions are retained; limiting current behavior governs continuous operation</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-1">Electrodialysis reversal periodically reverses polarity at minutes‑to‑hours timescales to reduce scaling/fouling and increase recovery compared to conventional ED</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-3">In EDI, an applied DC field causes water dissociation at the diluate to produce H+ and OH− that continuously regenerate the ion‑exchange resins, enabling electrochemical regeneration without chemical acid/base regeneration cycles</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-0">EDI modules operate under a constant electric field to continuously demineralize water using ion‑exchange resins, ion‑selective membranes, and avoid laborious acid/alkali regeneration</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-4">EDI systems are fully automated and achieve resistivity above 15 MΩ·cm for high‑purity water</cite>.

How ED enables continuous operation
- Electrically driven ionic transport across alternating cation/anion membranes creates selective permeation of counterions with retention of coions, producing deionized permeate continuously as long as gradients and applied field are maintained. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Alternating permselective cation and anion exchange membranes allow only cations or only anions to permeate while retaining coions, creating diluate and concentrate compartments and enabling continuous deionization under an applied electric field</cite>.
- Flow modes are designed for uptime: either continuous feed/through of water in the stack or recirculating loops, both eliminating the need for chemical steps and enabling variable‑power operation. <cite id="761c3f20-3">ED functions by flowing feed through spacers separated by ion‑exchange membranes under an electric field; it can be operated with continuous flow through the stack or with batches recirculating, and is inherently electrically driven with reduced energy/capital needs and long membrane lifetimes</cite>.
- Polarity reversal (EDR) and over‑limiting regimes provide operational levers for continuous, fouling‑resistant operation. <cite id="761c3f20-1">In ED/EDR, polarity is periodically reversed over minutes to hours to reverse ionic flow and improve fouling/scaling behavior and recovery; ED can also be operated at over‑limiting current to enhance mass transfer and reduce membrane area needs</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-0">Limiting current arises when interfacial concentration at the membrane–solution interface is much lower than bulk, saturating salt transport; ED operation and design manage this regime for continuous performance</cite>.
- Practical systems integrate ED upstream or downstream for continuous polishing. <cite id="761c3f20-2">A continuous hybrid process feeds streams to an ED‑deionization tank with constant flow, then continuously transfers the ED‑deionized stream to an EDI‑deionization tank, with continuous make‑up and product circulation to maintain stable, high‑purity product</cite>.

Why this avoids chemical regeneration cycles
- ED and EDI are membrane/field‑driven separations, not displacement softening. Ions are transported electrophoretically and by diffusion across permselective barriers; no external chemicals are used to displace counterions. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Under an applied field, cations/anions permeate their respective membranes while coions are retained, producing continuous deionization without chemical agents</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-3">ED is driven by an applied electric field rather than pressure, with continuous flow and long membrane durability</cite>.
- In EDI, the diluate channel contains ion‑exchange resin and operates at constant DC; water dissociation in the diluate generates H+ and OH− at the electrodes, which continuously restore mobile counter‑ion capacity in the resin (“internal regeneration”), eliminating acid/alkali regeneration cycles. <cite id="f4573fd8-3">EDI combines ion‑exchange resins and membranes; under DC, water dissociation produces H+ and OH− that continuously regenerate the resins without chemical regeneration</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-0">EDI modules combine speed/efficiency of ion exchange with absence of laborious acid/alkali regeneration, operating as a continuous demineralization process</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-1">EDI fills the diluate channel with resins to improve conductivity and avoid back‑diffusion, with water dissociation enabling self‑regeneration and aiding continuous operation</cite>.
- EDI can be configured as filled‑cell/continuous electrodeionization, which is functionally continuous and widely used to substitute mixed‑bed units in power and electronics applications. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Filled Cell Electrodialysis/Continuous Electrodeionization uses alternating membranes and continuous operation to produce pure or ultrapure water in food/pharmaceutical and regeneration applications</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-2">EDI substitutes mixed beds by avoiding chemical regeneration problems (waste handling, neutralization, logistics, semi‑automatic operation), and is essential as a polishing step after RO to reach resistivity >17 MΩ·cm</cite>.

Mechanisms that sustain continuous ultrapure product
- Membrane stacks and current control: Constant flows and voltage/field control maintain diluate concentration/product quality; automation and resistivity/UV monitoring close loops without batch stops. <cite id="f4573fd8-4">An EDI plant achieves resistivity above 15 MΩ·cm and is fully automated with online monitoring (pressure, flux, flow, resistivity), PLC control, and optional UV/mixed‑bed polishing</cite>.
- Over‑limiting operation and electroconvection: Operating beyond limiting current increases convective mass transfer, lowering required membrane area and enabling continuous high‑throughput demineralization; careful membrane design is needed to manage water splitting and fouling. <cite id="761c3f20-1">Operating ED at over‑limiting current increases mass transfer and reduces membrane area, while membrane structure modifications can enhance electroconvection and control water dissociation; however, higher dissociation and fouling/scaling must be managed</cite>.
- Bipolar and advanced ED variants: Bipolar‑membrane ED (EDBM) converts salts into acid/base streams, freeing permeate quality from electrode chemistry and enabling continuous high‑purity water; ED metathesis (EDM) swaps less soluble salts for more soluble ones in concentrate, enabling high recovery. <cite id="761c3f20-1">EDB uses bipolar membranes to convert salts into acids and bases; EDI dissociation enables continuous ultra‑pure water production</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-4">EDB converts salts into acids/bases, while EDM performs metathesis to precipitate salts in concentrate, enabling high water recovery</cite>.
- Hybrid ED+EDI polishing trains: ED provides primary deionization and flow control; EDI continuously polishes to sub‑µS/cm conductivities without chemical regeneration, with optional mixed‑bed/UV polishing only when needed. <cite id="f4573fd8-2">RO is followed by EDI to complete desalination and polish permeate; EDI cannot be simply replaced by two‑pass RO because it targets conductivities below 16 MΩ·cm, and EDI uses no chemical regeneration</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-2">A continuous process chain uses ED to deionize, then EDI to further deionize, with constant flows and make‑up to stabilize ultrapure product</cite>.

Performance and practical reach
- Final resistivity and speciation control: EDI trains routinely deliver >15–18 MΩ·cm, meeting boiler feed and electronics DI standards; ED alone or as first stage can meet partial demineralization before EDI polishing. <cite id="f4573fd8-0">Modern EDI installations obtain water with resistivity of 18 MΩ·cm, using continuous demineralization with ion‑exchange resins, membranes and a constant electric field</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-2">Boiler makeup requires resistivity >17 MΩ·cm; RO+EDI trains are industry‑proven to meet these limits, with EDI substituting mixed beds and avoiding chemical regeneration</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-4">EDI capacity up to 3400 l/h and fully automated monitoring/controls yields high‑purity product stored for distribution</cite>.
- Energy and maintenance: ED is compatible with variable renewable inputs (e.g., PV/wind), has long membrane life, and tolerates turbidity and chlorination, reducing OPEX and enabling continuous uptime. <cite id="761c3f20-3">ED adjusts to feedwater changes, handles higher turbidity and chlorine, exhibits 10–20+ year membrane lifetimes, and can operate with continuous flow or recirculation for reduced energy and maintenance</cite>.
- Hybrid reliability: Real processes combine ED and EDI with constant make‑up flows and optional polishing to maintain stable, continuous product, demonstrating that ED/EDI stacks can be designed for uninterrupted operation. <cite id="761c3f20-2">Continuous two‑step ED+EDI process maintains constant feed, deionization, and product flows, with make‑up water to control viscosity and ion concentrations, yielding stable ultrapure product</cite>.

Why “no chemical regeneration cycles” is achievable while conventional DI requires them
- Conventional mixed‑bed ion exchange operates in displacement mode: each cycle adds regenerant (acid/alkali) to displace counter‑ions, producing a batch product that must be drained/conditioned; ED/EDI replace displacement with field‑driven ion transport and internal electrochemical regeneration, enabling continuous permeate without batch regenerant additions. <cite id="f4573fd8-2">EDI substitutes mixed beds by avoiding problems of acid/alkali regeneration (chemical wastes, neutralization, logistics, semi‑automatic operation), and is essential for polishing to ultra‑pure quality</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-3">EDI’s continuous regeneration of ion‑exchange resins by electrochemical water dissociation eliminates chemical acid/base regeneration cycles</cite>.
- ED/EDI can integrate into RO‑based plants as a final polishing step, avoiding the need for multiple RO passes that would otherwise be required to reach equivalent resistivity, which are energy‑intensive and still not sufficient to reach 16 MΩ·cm+ consistently. <cite id="f4573fd8-2">Two‑pass RO approaches 1 µS·cm−1 but cannot reliably reach <0.0625 µS·cm−1 (18 MΩ·cm) and consumes more energy; EDI is unavoidable for preparation of make‑up water with resistivity >16 MΩ·cm</cite>.

Limitations and trade‑offs
- ED/EDI performance is bounded by limiting current, polarization, and water splitting; careful stack design, membrane chemistry, and operating regimes are needed to balance energy, product quality, and electrode/fouling risks. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Limiting current saturates salt transport at the membrane interface and constrains efficiency</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-1">Over‑limiting operation enhances mass transfer but increases water dissociation and fouling/scaling risks, requiring membrane design and control considerations</cite>.
- Achieving ultrapure water typically requires EDI or advanced ED configurations; while ED alone can demineralize, reaching 15–18 MΩ·cm often needs EDI polishing and ancillary steps (e.g., UV, mixed‑bed back‑up) to control TOC/SiO2/bacteria. <cite id="f4573fd8-4">High‑purity EDI product is stored and optionally recirculated through mixed resin bed and UV to further improve quality</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-2">Hybrid ED+EDI schemes incorporate additional make‑up and polishing flows to stabilize ultrapure product</cite>.

Bottom line
Continuous ultrapure water production without chemical regeneration is enabled by ED/EDI’s electric‑field coupling to ion transport and internal electrochemical regeneration: alternating permselective membranes (ED/EDR) and filled‑cell ED/EDI stacks maintain continuous deionization, with periodic polarity reversal and over‑limiting regimes ensuring stable, fouling‑resistant flow; EDI integrates water dissociation at the diluate to continuously restore resin capacity, eliminating acid/alkali regeneration, while automation and RO+EDI trains deliver >15–18 MΩ·cm product with minimal maintenance. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Alternating cation/anion membranes under applied fields create continuous deionization compartments and have long been used to produce pure/ultrapure water</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-1">EDR polarity reversal and EDI’s internal dissociation/self‑regeneration enable continuous operation and ultra‑pure water production</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-0">Modern EDI systems obtain 18 MΩ·cm water and avoid acid/alkali regeneration</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-2">EDI replaces mixed beds and is essential to reach resistivity >16–17 MΩ·cm without chemical regeneration cycles</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-4">Plants are fully automated and scalable, with EDI achieving resistivity above 15 MΩ·cm</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-3">ED’s electrically driven, variable‑power, continuous‑flow nature supports reliable, low‑OPEX uptime</cite>.

Title: Advancing electrodeionization with conductive ionomer binders that immobilize ion-exchange resin particles into porous wafer substrates
Snippet: Electrodeionization (EDI) is an electrically driven separations technology that employs ion-exchange membranes and resin particles. Deionization occurs under the influence of an applied electric field, facilitating continuous regeneration of the resins and supplementing ionic conductivity. While EDI is commercially used for ultrapure water production, material innovation is required for improving desalination performance and energy efficiency for treating alternative water supplies. This work reports a new class of ion-exchange resin-wafers (RWs) fabricated with ion-conductive binders that exhibit exceptional ionic conductivities—a 3–5-fold improvement over conventional RWs that contain a non-ionic polyethylene binder. Incorporation into an EDI stack (RW-EDI) resulted in an increased desalination rate and reduced energy expenditure compared to the conventional RWs. The water-splitting phenomenon was also investigated in the RW in an external experimental setup in this work. Overall, this work demonstrates that ohmic resistances can be substantially curtailed with ionomer binder RWs at dilute salt concentrations.

Snippet: Electrodeionization (EDI) combines the ion exchange resins (IER) and ion exchange membrane (IEM) to produce hydrogen ions (H þ ) and hydroxide ions (OH À ) in the water dissociation reaction under the action of a direct current electric field. The continuous regeneration of IER is implemented by electrochemical method without chemical regeneration (Arar et al. ). Thus, this novel and friendly separation process has been widely applied to industrial production, such as heavy metal recovery (Dermentzis et al. ; Lu et al. ), microelectronics, electric power, chemical industry (Strathmann ), and desalination (Wardani et al. ). But further research is still in progress for reducing energy consumption (Lee et  High energy consumption of the EDI process is a factor restricting its large-scale industrial application, because the acid and base generated by the regeneration process is not utilized effectively, which enormously impacts the regeneration efficiency of IER. Therefore, many efforts have been concentrated on regenerating IER efficiently (Jordan et al. ), in which reducing the overall stack resistance and enhancing water dissociation reaction are the main purpose (Hakim et al. ). For example, an IEM with high conductivity and high selectivity can reduce energy consumption as higher ionic transfer and lower stack resistance (Zhao et al. ). A narrow particle size distribution of IER exhibits a lower stack resistance and better ion transport than standard IER distribution (Lu et al. ). Besides, the water dissociation reaction in the separated-bed configuration can be enhanced by inserting a bipolar membrane between the two beds (Strathmann ; Lakehal & Bouhidel ). Although these methods have successfully enhanced the regeneration of IER, it is considered to be a more economical and effective method to enhance the regeneration of IER by changing the bed type (Jin et al. ). Notably, the regeneration efficiency of IER can be promoted by placing the same type of IER together (Golubenko et al. ). Consistent with the traditional bipolar membrane process, this method enhances water dissociation reaction, thus improving the regeneration efficiency of IER.

Summary answer
Electrodialysis achieves continuous ultrapure water production by using electric fields and ion‑selective membranes to drive continuous ionic transport and membrane polarization, with optional polarity reversal and over‑limiting regimes to maintain steady flow without batch stops; electrodeionization (EDI) further integrates ion‑exchange resins and membranes so that water dissociation at the diluate side electrochemically regenerates the resins continuously, eliminating the need for external acid/alkali regeneration cycles and enabling automated, hands‑off production of water with resistivity >15–18 MΩ·cm. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Continuous processes such as Electrodialysis and Filled‑Cell Electrodialysis/Continuous Electrodeionization use alternating cationic and anionic permselective membranes under an applied field to create diluate/concentrate compartments, with deionization occurring continuously as ions permeate while coions are retained; limiting current behavior governs continuous operation</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-1">Electrodialysis reversal periodically reverses polarity at minutes‑to‑hours timescales to reduce scaling/fouling and increase recovery compared to conventional ED</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-3">In EDI, an applied DC field causes water dissociation at the diluate to produce H+ and OH− that continuously regenerate the ion‑exchange resins, enabling electrochemical regeneration without chemical acid/base regeneration cycles</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-0">EDI modules operate under a constant electric field to continuously demineralize water using ion‑exchange resins, ion‑selective membranes, and avoid laborious acid/alkali regeneration</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-4">EDI systems are fully automated and achieve resistivity above 15 MΩ·cm for high‑purity water</cite>.

How ED enables continuous operation
- Electrically driven ionic transport across alternating cation/anion membranes creates selective permeation of counterions with retention of coions, producing deionized permeate continuously as long as gradients and applied field are maintained. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Alternating permselective cation and anion exchange membranes allow only cations or only anions to permeate while retaining coions, creating diluate and concentrate compartments and enabling continuous deionization under an applied electric field</cite>.
- Flow modes are designed for uptime: either continuous feed/through of water in the stack or recirculating loops, both eliminating the need for chemical steps and enabling variable‑power operation. <cite id="761c3f20-3">ED functions by flowing feed through spacers separated by ion‑exchange membranes under an electric field; it can be operated with continuous flow through the stack or with batches recirculating, and is inherently electrically driven with reduced energy/capital needs and long membrane lifetimes</cite>.
- Polarity reversal (EDR) and over‑limiting regimes provide operational levers for continuous, fouling‑resistant operation. <cite id="761c3f20-1">In ED/EDR, polarity is periodically reversed over minutes to hours to reverse ionic flow and improve fouling/scaling behavior and recovery; ED can also be operated at over‑limiting current to enhance mass transfer and reduce membrane area needs</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-0">Limiting current arises when interfacial concentration at the membrane–solution interface is much lower than bulk, saturating salt transport; ED operation and design manage this regime for continuous performance</cite>.
- Practical systems integrate ED upstream or downstream for continuous polishing. <cite id="761c3f20-2">A continuous hybrid process feeds streams to an ED‑deionization tank with constant flow, then continuously transfers the ED‑deionized stream to an EDI‑deionization tank, with continuous make‑up and product circulation to maintain stable, high‑purity product</cite>.

Why this avoids chemical regeneration cycles
- ED and EDI are membrane/field‑driven separations, not displacement softening. Ions are transported electrophoretically and by diffusion across permselective barriers; no external chemicals are used to displace counterions. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Under an applied field, cations/anions permeate their respective membranes while coions are retained, producing continuous deionization without chemical agents</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-3">ED is driven by an applied electric field rather than pressure, with continuous flow and long membrane durability</cite>.
- In EDI, the diluate channel contains ion‑exchange resin and operates at constant DC; water dissociation in the diluate generates H+ and OH− at the electrodes, which continuously restore mobile counter‑ion capacity in the resin (“internal regeneration”), eliminating acid/alkali regeneration cycles. <cite id="f4573fd8-3">EDI combines ion‑exchange resins and membranes; under DC, water dissociation produces H+ and OH− that continuously regenerate the resins without chemical regeneration</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-0">EDI modules combine speed/efficiency of ion exchange with absence of laborious acid/alkali regeneration, operating as a continuous demineralization process</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-1">EDI fills the diluate channel with resins to improve conductivity and avoid back‑diffusion, with water dissociation enabling self‑regeneration and aiding continuous operation</cite>.
- EDI can be configured as filled‑cell/continuous electrodeionization, which is functionally continuous and widely used to substitute mixed‑bed units in power and electronics applications. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Filled Cell Electrodialysis/Continuous Electrodeionization uses alternating membranes and continuous operation to produce pure or ultrapure water in food/pharmaceutical and regeneration applications</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-2">EDI substitutes mixed beds by avoiding chemical regeneration problems (waste handling, neutralization, logistics, semi‑automatic operation), and is essential as a polishing step after RO to reach resistivity >17 MΩ·cm</cite>.

Mechanisms that sustain continuous ultrapure product
- Membrane stacks and current control: Constant flows and voltage/field control maintain diluate concentration/product quality; automation and resistivity/UV monitoring close loops without batch stops. <cite id="f4573fd8-4">An EDI plant achieves resistivity above 15 MΩ·cm and is fully automated with online monitoring (pressure, flux, flow, resistivity), PLC control, and optional UV/mixed‑bed polishing</cite>.
- Over‑limiting operation and electroconvection: Operating beyond limiting current increases convective mass transfer, lowering required membrane area and enabling continuous high‑throughput demineralization; careful membrane design is needed to manage water splitting and fouling. <cite id="761c3f20-1">Operating ED at over‑limiting current increases mass transfer and reduces membrane area, while membrane structure modifications can enhance electroconvection and control water dissociation; however, higher dissociation and fouling/scaling must be managed</cite>.
- Bipolar and advanced ED variants: Bipolar‑membrane ED (EDBM) converts salts into acid/base streams, freeing permeate quality from electrode chemistry and enabling continuous high‑purity water; ED metathesis (EDM) swaps less soluble salts for more soluble ones in concentrate, enabling high recovery. <cite id="761c3f20-1">EDB uses bipolar membranes to convert salts into acids and bases; EDI dissociation enables continuous ultra‑pure water production</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-4">EDB converts salts into acids/bases, while EDM performs metathesis to precipitate salts in concentrate, enabling high water recovery</cite>.
- Hybrid ED+EDI polishing trains: ED provides primary deionization and flow control; EDI continuously polishes to sub‑µS/cm conductivities without chemical regeneration, with optional mixed‑bed/UV polishing only when needed. <cite id="f4573fd8-2">RO is followed by EDI to complete desalination and polish permeate; EDI cannot be simply replaced by two‑pass RO because it targets conductivities below 16 MΩ·cm, and EDI uses no chemical regeneration</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-2">A continuous process chain uses ED to deionize, then EDI to further deionize, with constant flows and make‑up to stabilize ultrapure product</cite>.

Performance and practical reach
- Final resistivity and speciation control: EDI trains routinely deliver >15–18 MΩ·cm, meeting boiler feed and electronics DI standards; ED alone or as first stage can meet partial demineralization before EDI polishing. <cite id="f4573fd8-0">Modern EDI installations obtain water with resistivity of 18 MΩ·cm, using continuous demineralization with ion‑exchange resins, membranes and a constant electric field</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-2">Boiler makeup requires resistivity >17 MΩ·cm; RO+EDI trains are industry‑proven to meet these limits, with EDI substituting mixed beds and avoiding chemical regeneration</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-4">EDI capacity up to 3400 l/h and fully automated monitoring/controls yields high‑purity product stored for distribution</cite>.
- Energy and maintenance: ED is compatible with variable renewable inputs (e.g., PV/wind), has long membrane life, and tolerates turbidity and chlorination, reducing OPEX and enabling continuous uptime. <cite id="761c3f20-3">ED adjusts to feedwater changes, handles higher turbidity and chlorine, exhibits 10–20+ year membrane lifetimes, and can operate with continuous flow or recirculation for reduced energy and maintenance</cite>.
- Hybrid reliability: Real processes combine ED and EDI with constant make‑up flows and optional polishing to maintain stable, continuous product, demonstrating that ED/EDI stacks can be designed for uninterrupted operation. <cite id="761c3f20-2">Continuous two‑step ED+EDI process maintains constant feed, deionization, and product flows, with make‑up water to control viscosity and ion concentrations, yielding stable ultrapure product</cite>.

Why “no chemical regeneration cycles” is achievable while conventional DI requires them
- Conventional mixed‑bed ion exchange operates in displacement mode: each cycle adds regenerant (acid/alkali) to displace counter‑ions, producing a batch product that must be drained/conditioned; ED/EDI replace displacement with field‑driven ion transport and internal electrochemical regeneration, enabling continuous permeate without batch regenerant additions. <cite id="f4573fd8-2">EDI substitutes mixed beds by avoiding problems of acid/alkali regeneration (chemical wastes, neutralization, logistics, semi‑automatic operation), and is essential for polishing to ultra‑pure quality</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-3">EDI’s continuous regeneration of ion‑exchange resins by electrochemical water dissociation eliminates chemical acid/base regeneration cycles</cite>.
- ED/EDI can integrate into RO‑based plants as a final polishing step, avoiding the need for multiple RO passes that would otherwise be required to reach equivalent resistivity, which are energy‑intensive and still not sufficient to reach 16 MΩ·cm+ consistently. <cite id="f4573fd8-2">Two‑pass RO approaches 1 µS·cm−1 but cannot reliably reach <0.0625 µS·cm−1 (18 MΩ·cm) and consumes more energy; EDI is unavoidable for preparation of make‑up water with resistivity >16 MΩ·cm</cite>.

Limitations and trade‑offs
- ED/EDI performance is bounded by limiting current, polarization, and water splitting; careful stack design, membrane chemistry, and operating regimes are needed to balance energy, product quality, and electrode/fouling risks. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Limiting current saturates salt transport at the membrane interface and constrains efficiency</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-1">Over‑limiting operation enhances mass transfer but increases water dissociation and fouling/scaling risks, requiring membrane design and control considerations</cite>.
- Achieving ultrapure water typically requires EDI or advanced ED configurations; while ED alone can demineralize, reaching 15–18 MΩ·cm often needs EDI polishing and ancillary steps (e.g., UV, mixed‑bed back‑up) to control TOC/SiO2/bacteria. <cite id="f4573fd8-4">High‑purity EDI product is stored and optionally recirculated through mixed resin bed and UV to further improve quality</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-2">Hybrid ED+EDI schemes incorporate additional make‑up and polishing flows to stabilize ultrapure product</cite>.

Bottom line
Continuous ultrapure water production without chemical regeneration is enabled by ED/EDI’s electric‑field coupling to ion transport and internal electrochemical regeneration: alternating permselective membranes (ED/EDR) and filled‑cell ED/EDI stacks maintain continuous deionization, with periodic polarity reversal and over‑limiting regimes ensuring stable, fouling‑resistant flow; EDI integrates water dissociation at the diluate to continuously restore resin capacity, eliminating acid/alkali regeneration, while automation and RO+EDI trains deliver >15–18 MΩ·cm product with minimal maintenance. <cite id="761c3f20-0">Alternating cation/anion membranes under applied fields create continuous deionization compartments and have long been used to produce pure/ultrapure water</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-1">EDR polarity reversal and EDI’s internal dissociation/self‑regeneration enable continuous operation and ultra‑pure water production</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-0">Modern EDI systems obtain 18 MΩ·cm water and avoid acid/alkali regeneration</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-2">EDI replaces mixed beds and is essential to reach resistivity >16–17 MΩ·cm without chemical regeneration cycles</cite> <cite id="f4573fd8-4">Plants are fully automated and scalable, with EDI achieving resistivity above 15 MΩ·cm</cite> <cite id="761c3f20-3">ED’s electrically driven, variable‑power, continuous‑flow nature supports reliable, low‑OPEX uptime</cite>.</answer>

Title: A new process for desalination and electrodeionization of water by means of electrostatic shielding zones - ionic current sinks.
Snippet: Intensive industrialization and the associated water pollution compose a gradually increasing threat of fresh water shortage in many areas of the world. Purification of used, polluted and contaminated water or desalination of brackish and seawater have recently won an increased technological interest which apparently will become more urgent in the not distant future. 

Deionization (DI) is the removal of ions and ionizable species from water or organic liquids and may be achieved by various techniques, such as Ion Exchange (IE), Reverse Osmosis (RO), Distillation and Electrodeionization (EDI). EDI uses electrically active media and an electrical potential to cause ion transport and may be operated batch wise, or continuously. 

Continuous processes such as Electrodialysis [1,2], Electrodialysis Reversal [3], and Filled Cell Electrodialysis or otherwise called Continuous Electrodeionization [4,5] comprise alternating permselective cation exchange membranes and anion exchange membranes, which under the influence of the electric field allow only cations or only anions respectively to permeate their mass and simultaneously retain coions so that diluate and concentrate compartments are created and deionization occurs. 

Electrodialysis has been successfully performed over the last decades mainly in the production of potable water from brackish or seawater [6], regeneration of ion exchange resins [4,5] and production of pure or ultrapure water, demineralization and deacidification in food or pharmaceutical processing [7], purification of radioactive waste water in nuclear power plants [8] and recovery of water and valuable metals from industrial effluents [9][10][11][12][13]. 

Electrodialysis is an ecologically expedient and economically profitable method of water demineralization. However, the efficiency of the method is limited by the so called limiting current density [14][15][16][17][18][19] which is the state where the electrolyte concentration at the membranesolution interface reaches values much less than in the bulk solution. In this state the salt ion current reaches its saturation and does not grow with voltage increase.

ED functions by flowing feed solution through a stack of spacers, each separated by selectively charged cation and anion exchange membranes (Fig. 1). An applied electric field drives the transport of ions across these membranes. The process is operated with either continuous flow of water through the stack or via batches of water recirculating through the stack 27 . This electrically driven-rather than pressure-driven-process causes reduced energy consumption 28 and cost 29 in brackish water and partial desalination scenarios. The energy efficiency of ED reduces solar or wind array sizes and thus capital cost and system footprint. The high water efficiency of ED is especially beneficial in water stressed regions 6 ; this feature reduces brine volume, which is often challenging to manage and a relatively large source of operational costs 30 . Moreover, ED exhibits the capability to adjust to changes in feedwater concentration and modify the target output concentration. ED can effectively manage feedwater with higher turbidity, and its membranes can endure exposure to chlorine, commonly utilized for disinfection and antifouling purposes 31 . Notably, ED membrane lifetimes can extend to 10-20+ years and demonstrate resilience to a wide range of pH and temperature fluctuations 32 . These characteristics of ED collectively contribute to a reduction in maintenance and OPEX, proving especially valuable in decentralized, resource-constrained scenarios. 

A key feature of ED that makes it well suited for renewable desalination is the ability to operate at variable power levels 33 , which can aid in reducing or eliminating the need for energy storage. Title: Frontiers of Membrane Desalination Processes for Brackish Water Treatment: A Review
Snippet: Since the first commercial ED plant in the 1950s, a number of ED-based processes have been developed, including electrodialysis reversal (EDR) [275], bipolar membrane electrodialysis (EDBM) [276], electro-deionization (EDI) [277], electrodialysis metathesis (EDM) [278], and RED [279]. In EDR, the polarity of the power source is periodically reversed at intervals between a few minutes to a few hours, reversing the ionic flow direction. EDR is a commercialized process with a lower fouling and scaling potential and higher water recovery compared to ED. EDBM takes advantage of bipolar membranes and converts salts into acids and bases. In EDI, the diluate channel is filled with ion exchange resins to improve the conductivity of the solution and avoid the back-diffusion of ions from the concentrate channel. Water dissociation in the diluate channel can result in the self-regeneration of ion exchange resins and aid in the continuous operation of the process. EDI is used for ultra-pure water production. EDM is a novel alteration of ED in which metathesis reactions take place to convert less soluble salts to more soluble species. The repeating unit cell contains four compartments (quad) with two diluate and two concentrate channels. Feed water enters one of the diluate channels and the substituting solution enters the other. Non-precipitating salts are formed in the concentrate compartments. In EDM, high water recovery can be reached, decreasing the volume of the concentrate waste stream and enhancing the ability to produce salts. RED is a technique to harvest salinity gradient energy (blue energy) from the mixing of two streams with different salt content [279]. Blue energy is not affected by seasonal changes, unlike solar and wind, and can serve as a source of renewable energy. The development of these ED-based processes can broaden the applications of the processes for a wider range of feed water quality. However, further research should be conducted on these novel processes to improve the operational conditions, as well as on the membrane and electrode materials to enhance their energy-and cost-effectiveness.

snippet.text:
Intensive industrialization and the associated water pollution compose a gradually increasing threat of fresh water shortage in many areas of the world. Purification of used, polluted and contaminated water or desalination of brackish and seawater have recently won an increased technological interest which apparently will become more urgent in the not distant future. 

Deionization (DI) is the removal of ions and ionizable species from water or organic liquids and may be achieved by various techniques, such as Ion Exchange (IE), Reverse Osmosis (RO), Distillation and Electrodeionization (EDI). EDI uses electrically active media and an electrical potential to cause ion transport and may be operated batch wise, or continuously. 

Continuous processes such as Electrodialysis [1,2], Electrodialysis Reversal [3], and Filled Cell Electrodialysis or otherwise called Continuous Electrodeionization [4,5] comprise alternating permselective cation exchange membranes and anion exchange membranes, which under the influence of the electric field allow only cations or only anions respectively to permeate their mass and simultaneously retain coions so that diluate and concentrate compartments are created and deionization occurs. 

Electrodialysis has been successfully performed over the last decades mainly in the production of potable water from brackish or seawater [6], regeneration of ion exchange resins [4,5] and production of pure or ultrapure water, demineralization and deacidification in food or pharmaceutical processing [7], purification of radioactive waste water in nuclear power plants [8] and recovery of water and valuable metals from industrial effluents [9][10][11][12][13]. 

Electrodialysis is an ecologically expedient and economically profitable method of water demineralization. However, the efficiency of the method is limited by the so called limiting current density [14][15][16][17][18][19] which is the state where the electrolyte concentration at the membranesolution interface reaches values much less than in the bulk solution. In this state the salt ion current reaches its saturation and does not grow with voltage increase.

Process 2 (Fig. 2) shows the continuous two-step electrodialysis separation process for the sugar and Ge-132 (NaOH) combining ED and EDI. In advance, as initial solutions (0 h) of the deionized solution and the concentrated solution, 1 L of each solution prepared in the preliminary test was added to the tank (D1, C1, D2, and C2). The isomerization reaction mixture supplied (150 mL/h) to the EDdeionization tank (D1) was deionized continuously by electrodialysis using ED. Distilled water was constantly supplied (330 mL/h) to D1 to reduce the viscosity of the solution. In conjunction with electrodialysis, the ED-deionized sugar solution was continuously supplied (300 mL/h) from D1 to the EDI-deionization tank (D2) and further deionized by electrodialysis using EDI. Distilled water was constantly supplied (120 mL/h) to the EDI-concentration tank (C2) to reduce the ion concentration of the solution. To facilitate dilution and collect the concentrated Ge-132, the EDI-recovery solution in C2 was continuously fed (120 mL/h) to the ED-concentration tank (C1), and the recovery solution in C1 was fed (300 mL/h) to the 10 L storage tank (S3) during electrodialysis. The deionized sugar solution in D2 was fed (300 mL/h) to the 100 mL storage tank (S1) during electrodialysis. Approximately 50 mL of the solution was stored in S1, and the feed (300 mL/h) was then started to process 3. 

Process 3 (Fig. 2) shows the continuous purification process employed for the sugar solution based on the use of an ion exchange resin. The deionized sugar solution (in S1) was purified by passing successively through one sodium adsorption column and two switchable Ge-132 adsorption columns and then fed (300 mL/h) to the 5 L storage tank (S2).

Title: Advancing electrodeionization with conductive ionomer binders that immobilize ion-exchange resin particles into porous wafer substrates
Snippet: Electrodeionization (EDI) is an electrically driven separations technology that employs ion-exchange membranes and resin particles. Deionization occurs under the influence of an applied electric field, facilitating continuous regeneration of the resins and supplementing ionic conductivity. While EDI is commercially used for ultrapure water production, material innovation is required for improving desalination performance and energy efficiency for treating alternative water supplies. This work reports a new class of ion-exchange resin-wafers (RWs) fabricated with ion-conductive binders that exhibit exceptional ionic conductivities—a 3–5-fold improvement over conventional RWs that contain a non-ionic polyethylene binder. Incorporation into an EDI stack (RW-EDI) resulted in an increased desalination rate and reduced energy expenditure compared to the conventional RWs. The water-splitting phenomenon was also investigated in the RW in an external experimental setup in this work. Overall, this work demonstrates that ohmic resistances can be substantially curtailed with ionomer binder RWs at dilute salt concentrations.

Title: State-of-the-Art Water Treatment in Czech Power Sector: Industry-Proven Case Studies Showing Economic and Technical Benefits of Membrane and Other Novel Technologies for Each Particular Water Cycle
Snippet: The most important case study was carried out on the make-up water for boilers. This water represents the highest standards of quality and strict limits of conductivity, concentration of ions, suspended and colloidal solids and dissolved gasses, as determined by national or European standards (in the European Union) [12]. The conductivity of make-up water for high-pressure boilers should be as close as possible to theoretical water (i.e., clear water containing just H 2 O) exhibiting a resistivity of more than 17 MΩ cm −1 . The arrangement of membrane units in the pilot test was inspired by the combination of membrane processes commonly used in western European countries. These consist of ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis and electrodeionization. The main purpose of an ultrafiltration unit is to decrease the silt density index (SDI 15 < 5) before feeding the reverse osmosis. The reverse osmosis substitutes classical ion exchange demineralization units. The downstream electrodeionization unit then completes the desalination process and polishes the water.

The technology of electrodeionization substitutes mixed beds, because it avoids the additional problems with the chemicals used in the regeneration of mixed beds (e.g., liquid wastes, neutralization of wastes), administration, the transportation of chemicals and wastes, large built-up area, semi-automatic operation, etc. Electrodeionization (EDI) is intended for polishing the reverse osmosis (RO) permeate. It is an essential process which cannot be simply substituted by two-pass (or more) reverse osmosis. The two-pass reverse osmosis usually serves for sequential decarbonization and desilication. The conductivity of the osmosis permeate from the second pass is approximately 1 µS cm −1 . The energy consumption of two-pass reverse osmosis is higher in comparison with electrodeionization, and the recovery rate is also lower. Two-pass reverse osmosis is used when the hardness of raw water is too high, or when we want to achieve a water quality after electrodeionization that is better than 16 MΩ cm −1 (<0.0625 µS cm −1 ). Title: An innovative compound bed of EDI device with enhancing ion-exchange resins regeneration efficiency.
Snippet: Electrodeionization (EDI) combines the ion exchange resins (IER) and ion exchange membrane (IEM) to produce hydrogen ions (H þ ) and hydroxide ions (OH À ) in the water dissociation reaction under the action of a direct current electric field. The continuous regeneration of IER is implemented by electrochemical method without chemical regeneration (Arar et al. ). Thus, this novel and friendly separation process has been widely applied to industrial production, such as heavy metal recovery (Dermentzis et al. ; Lu et al. ), microelectronics, electric power, chemical industry (Strathmann ), and desalination (Wardani et al. ). But further research is still in progress for reducing energy consumption (Lee et  High energy consumption of the EDI process is a factor restricting its large-scale industrial application, because the acid and base generated by the regeneration process is not utilized effectively, which enormously impacts the regeneration efficiency of IER. Therefore, many efforts have been concentrated on regenerating IER efficiently (Jordan et al. ), in which reducing the overall stack resistance and enhancing water dissociation reaction are the main purpose (Hakim et al. ). For example, an IEM with high conductivity and high selectivity can reduce energy consumption as higher ionic transfer and lower stack resistance (Zhao et al. ). A narrow particle size distribution of IER exhibits a lower stack resistance and better ion transport than standard IER distribution (Lu et al. ). Besides, the water dissociation reaction in the separated-bed configuration can be enhanced by inserting a bipolar membrane between the two beds (Strathmann ; Lakehal & Bouhidel ). Although these methods have successfully enhanced the regeneration of IER, it is considered to be a more economical and effective method to enhance the regeneration of IER by changing the bed type (Jin et al. ). Notably, the regeneration efficiency of IER can be promoted by placing the same type of IER together (Golubenko et al. ). Consistent with the traditional bipolar membrane process, this method enhances water dissociation reaction, thus improving the regeneration efficiency of IER.

snippet.text: Electrodeionization (EDI) is an electrically driven separations technology that employs ion-exchange membranes and resin particles. Deionization occurs under the influence of an applied electric field, facilitating continuous regeneration of the resins and supplementing ionic conductivity. While EDI is commercially used for ultrapure water production, material innovation is required for improving desalination performance and energy efficiency for treating alternative water supplies. This work reports a new class of ion-exchange resin-wafers (RWs) fabricated with ion-conductive binders that exhibit exceptional ionic conductivities—a 3–5-fold improvement over conventional RWs that contain a non-ionic polyethylene binder. Incorporation into an EDI stack (RW-EDI) resulted in an increased desalination rate and reduced energy expenditure compared to the conventional RWs. The water-splitting phenomenon was also investigated in the RW in an external experimental setup in this work. Overall, this work demonstrates that ohmic resistances can be substantially curtailed with ionomer binder RWs at dilute salt concentrations.

snippet.text: Electrodeionization (EDI) combines the ion exchange resins (IER) and ion exchange membrane (IEM) to produce hydrogen ions (H þ ) and hydroxide ions (OH À ) in the water dissociation reaction under the action of a direct current electric field. The continuous regeneration of IER is implemented by electrochemical method without chemical regeneration (Arar et al. ). Thus, this novel and friendly separation process has been widely applied to industrial production, such as heavy metal recovery (Dermentzis et al. ; Lu et al. ), microelectronics, electric power, chemical industry (Strathmann ), and desalination (Wardani et al. ). But further research is still in progress for reducing energy consumption (Lee et  High energy consumption of the EDI process is a factor restricting its large-scale industrial application, because the acid and base generated by the regeneration process is not utilized effectively, which enormously impacts the regeneration efficiency of IER. Therefore, many efforts have been concentrated on regenerating IER efficiently (Jordan et al. ), in which reducing the overall stack resistance and enhancing water dissociation reaction are the main purpose (Hakim et al. ). For example, an IEM with high conductivity and high selectivity can reduce energy consumption as higher ionic transfer and lower stack resistance (Zhao et al. ). A narrow particle size distribution of IER exhibits a lower stack resistance and better ion transport than standard IER distribution (Lu et al. ). Besides, the water dissociation reaction in the separated-bed configuration can be enhanced by inserting a bipolar membrane between the two beds (Strathmann ; Lakehal & Bouhidel ). Although these methods have successfully enhanced the regeneration of IER, it is considered to be a more economical and effective method to enhance the regeneration of IER by changing the bed type (Jin et al. ). Notably, the regeneration efficiency of IER can be promoted by placing the same type of IER together (Golubenko et al. ). Consistent with the traditional bipolar membrane process, this method enhances water dissociation reaction, thus improving the regeneration efficiency of IER.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer correctly distinguishes between conventional electrodialysis (ED) and electrodeionization (EDI). It explicitly states that EDI 'integrates ion‑exchange resins and membranes so that water dissociation at the diluate side electrochemically regenerates the resins continuously, eliminating the need for external acid/alkali regeneration cycles.' It acknowledges that conventional ED requires polarity reversal (EDR) for fouling management ('EDR polarity reversal' and 'periodically reverses polarity at minutes‑to‑hours timescales to reduce scaling/fouling'). The answer clearly identifies EDI as the technology that achieves truly continuous operation without chemical regeneration through continuous electrochemical resin regeneration, and provides multiple citations distinguishing the regeneration mechanisms of ED versus EDI.
other_issues: The answer is excessively verbose and repetitive, making it difficult to extract the core distinction quickly. The summary answer itself is a 4-line run-on sentence.

The structure conflates ED and EDI in several places despite technically distinguishing them—the question asks specifically about 'electrodialysis' but the correct answer is that it's EDI, not ED, that meets the constraint. The answer should more directly state upfront that the premise is partially incorrect.

Some citations appear to be paraphrased in ways that may overstate their content (e.g., 'Continuous processes such as Electrodialysis and Filled‑Cell Electrodialysis/Continuous Electrodeionization' suggests the source treats these as equivalent 'continuous processes' without regeneration, which may not be accurate).

The section 'How ED enables continuous operation' could mislead readers into thinking standard ED achieves the 'no chemical regeneration' goal, when in fact ED still requires periodic interventions (polarity reversal, cleaning) and doesn't achieve ultrapure water on its own.

The 'Bottom line' again conflates ED and EDI by saying 'Continuous ultrapure water production without chemical regeneration is enabled by ED/EDI' when only EDI truly eliminates chemical regeneration cycles.
judgment.summary: The answer satisfies the verification criterion by correctly distinguishing ED from EDI and identifying that EDI (not conventional ED) achieves continuous operation without chemical regeneration through electrochemical resin regeneration. However, the answer suffers from excessive verbosity, structural issues that conflate the two technologies in several sections, and a lack of directness in correcting the premise of the question. The core technical content is sound and properly cited, but the presentation obscures the key distinction.

The previous attempt was passed because although the answer was verbose and conflated ED/EDI structurally, it did technically identify that EDI (not ED) meets the 'continuous without regeneration' requirement. The judge noted the system successfully retrieved the distinguishing facts even if presentation was messy. To make it harder, I need a question where correct retrieval alone is insufficient—the system must perform reasoning that the literature doesn't do for it.

Options:
1. Multi-step quantitative reasoning: Ask about concentration polarization limits across different membrane configurations, requiring the system to synthesize numbers from separate papers. But these might be directly stated in reviews.

2. Temporal contradiction exploitation: Ask about efficiency changes over time in a way that forces reconciling conflicting reported trends. But electrodialysis literature may not have clean contradictions the way sparse attention does.

3. Mechanistic causal reasoning: Ask WHY a phenomenon occurs when papers describe THAT it occurs but don't explain the mechanism, requiring the system to infer causality. For instance, why does current efficiency decrease at high current density? Papers report this empirically but explaining it requires connecting separate concepts (water splitting, co-ion leakage, concentration polarization) that aren't packaged as 'the explanation.'

4. False equivalence requiring mechanistic distinction: The previous attempt used operational distinction (continuous vs periodic). Instead, embed a false mechanistic equivalence: assert that two phenomena are 'the same underlying mechanism' when they're actually distinct but superficially similar. For electrodialysis: water splitting at membranes vs. electrolysis at electrodes—both involve water decomposition and ion generation, both occur in ED stacks, but they're different phenomena with different causes and impacts. Literature discusses each separately but doesn't explicitly contrast them as 'not the same mechanism' because no one claims they are.

5. Constraint that requires integrating non-obvious scaling laws: Ask about performance under conditions that require combining multiple factors (concentration, current, membrane area) that papers report independently but not in the specific combination asked.

attempts.answer:
Below is a mechanistic view of how water splitting at ion‑exchange membranes (IEMs) couples to electrolysis at the electrodes in electrodialysis (ED) and related modes.

Overview: ED stacks and electrodes
In ED, an anode and cathode apply a potential across alternating cation‑exchange (CEM) and anion‑exchange membranes (AEM), driving cations to the cathode and anions to the anode; transport is limited by diffusion/adsorption at selective interfaces and by electric fields and convection in the boundary layers near membranes. <cite id="1b7a0116-3">Anions move toward the anode and cations toward the cathode, but are blocked at the first selective membrane they meet, creating a sequence of diluted and concentrated compartments in a stack of alternating CEM/AEM</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-3">Polarity reversal (EDR) flips the stack to increase membrane life and achieve higher recoveries</cite>. At the electrodes, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at the cathode and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) at the anode define the minimum thermodynamic driving force of about 1.23 V and impose additional overpotentials that depend on kinetics and mass transport. <cite id="6392c2ab-1">In ED, the hydrogen evolution reaction occurs at the cathode and the oxygen evolution reaction at the anode; the inherent potential drop is 1.23 V, but the actual initiation potential is higher, with overpotentials calculable via Tafel behavior</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-4">HER proceeds via a two‑electron transfer in alkaline AEMWE, whereas OER involves a four‑electron process with multiple proton–electron steps and sluggish kinetics, often rate‑limiting</cite>.

Water splitting at ion‑exchange membranes: catalytic and field‑driven mechanisms
Under moderate to high current densities, water can split at the surfaces and interfaces of IEMs, generating mobile H+ and OH− that affect ion transport and current efficiency. <cite id="1b7a0116-4">Water splitting in systems with IEMs is observed and arises from two mechanisms: catalytic dissociation/association on membrane ionic sites (proton transport between charged groups on AEMs) and non‑catalytic, field‑limited dissociation in expanded space‑charge regions where electric fields reach values that pull H and OH apart at maximum speed; WS is stronger on AEMs than CEMs</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-0">Decreasing water splitting rate at anion‑exchange membranes is key to improving overlimiting ED; a synergistic improvement arises when CEMs are optimized to enhance electroconvection and AEMs are optimized to suppress unwanted WS</cite>. At the microscopic scale near membranes, partial charge equilibrium breaks down in depleted diffusion layers, enabling coupled WS and ion transport to carry current; models based on the Nernst–Planck–Poisson framework capture how H+/OH− generated by WS modify fields and ion fluxes and why WS can both aid transport and reduce efficiency by promoting precipitation. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">Water splitting and electroconvection are the main phenomena affecting ion transfer in intensive current regimes; models that couple Nernst–Planck and Poisson equations across an electroneutral region, expanded space‑charge region, and quasi‑equilibrium surface zone reproduce ion concentrations and potential drops and show that, under the same current density, the surface space‑charge density at an AEM is lower than at a CEM, explaining how WS partially suppresses electroconvection and reduces salt ion transfer while transporting H+/OH−</cite>. Electrochemical impedance analyses also identify distinct electrical signatures of WS at AEM/solution and bipolar junctions. <cite id="1b7a0116-3">One sub‑arc corresponds to water splitting at the AEM/depleted solution interface, and another to water splitting at the bipolar junction</cite>.

How water splitting at membranes drives electrolysis at the electrodes
1) Charge accumulation and depletion near electrodes trigger WS and electrolysis. As cations accumulate at the cathode and anions at the anode under applied bias, local space‑charge and strong electric fields develop in depleted boundary layers, which can activate both catalytic and non‑catalytic WS. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">In the depleted diffusion boundary layer near an IEM, partial local electroneutrality breaks down, creating an expanded space‑charge region and quasi‑equilibrium surface zone where H+ and OH− generated by WS contribute to transport and modify the field structure</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-4">In such regions, fields can reach values sufficient to split water non‑catalytically at maximum speed, providing additional mobile carriers that screen charge and sustain current</cite>. These extra carriers couple to the electrode reactions: electrons supplied by the cathode reduce H+ (from WS or from migrated counterions) to H2 (HER), while electrons supplied to the anode oxidize OH− (from WS or from transported coions) to O2 (OER), thus manifesting electrolysis at the electrodes supported by membrane‑interface water splitting. <cite id="6392c2ab-1">The cathode HER and anode OER contribute potential drops whose thermodynamic minimum is 1.23 V and whose actual onset potentials exceed this value due to overpotentials that scale with current density via Tafel behavior</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-4">Because OER kinetics are intrinsically slower than HER, the anode often limits the overall cell voltage</cite>.

2) Coupled transport: membranes set directionality and selectivity that focus electrolysis where the field peaks. CEMs transmit H+ (or cations) and AEMs transmit OH− (or anions); under field reversal during EDR, roles swap. <cite id="6392c2ab-3">In ED, cations are blocked by the first AEM and anions by the first CEM; in EDR, polarity reversal of the stack allows net transport of counterions to the opposite electrodes and higher recoveries</cite>. Because membrane permselectivity and boundary‑layer depletion create strong internal fields near interfaces, the water splitting that occurs in the quasi‑equilibrium surface zones and bipolar regions supplies the mobile protons and hydroxides that neutralize local charge and shuttle to electrodes, where they participate in HER/OER and produce gas. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">A model that includes WS‑transported H+ and OH− across the depleted DBL shows how their current can be a significant fraction of total, even as WS reduces efficiency by precipitating sparingly soluble species</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-0">In overlimiting regimes, suppressing excessive WS at AEMs while enhancing CEM electroconvection is necessary to maintain high current without salt precipitation</cite>.

3) ED/EDR as intermittent electrolysis: polarity reversal alternately makes one electrode cathodic and anodic, so that each electrode periodically performs HER and OER. <cite id="6392c2ab-3">EDR reverses the polarity of the stack at set intervals; this extends membrane life and enables higher recoveries by periodically switching which side is anode and cathode</cite>. During the intervals when a given compartment is cathodic, cations accumulate at that electrode and the opposite anode, driving O2 evolution there; during the next interval, roles reverse and H2 evolution predominates at the same electrode. Membrane water splitting at the interfaces adjacent to the now‑reversed anode/cathode supports the corresponding electrolysis step by supplying H+/OH− to stabilize current and buffer pH near the electrodes. <cite id="1b7a0116-4">Field‑driven non‑catalytic water dissociation in expanded space‑charge regions at the membrane surfaces enables rapid generation of H+ and OH− under high fields, which can assist current transport during polarity reversal</cite>.

Bipolar‑membrane configurations decouple and optimize water splitting at the electrodes
When bipolar membranes (BPMs) are introduced, a junction of cation‑ and anion‑exchange layers creates a built‑in depletion region and strong internal electric field that preferentially dissociates water at the “bipolar junction,” producing H+ and OH− that migrate into adjacent compartments. <cite id="2247b294-2">A bipolar membrane consists of a cation‑exchange and an anion‑exchange layer laminated together; the junction, or bipolar interface, acts like a p–n junction, generating a depletion region and large electric field where water dissociation catalysts, if present, accelerate the splitting to produce H+ and OH− that migrate to opposite sides, enabling highly acidic and basic compartments with a large pH gradient</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-4">Under reverse bias (CEL to cathode, AEL to anode), migrating ions first move into bulk, then water at the interfacial layer polarizes and dissociates to generate H+ and OH−, which diffuse into adjacent compartments to create acidic and basic environments; this allows distinct pH optimization for OER and HER and reduces overall cell voltage for water splitting</cite>. In this architecture, the membrane‑driven water dissociation at the junction provides the charge carriers that traverse the membranes, while the electrodes operate at their kinetically favorable pH: OER in a relatively mild‑oxidation potential basic environment and HER in an acidic environment, minimizing the extra potential required beyond 1.23 V. <cite id="2247b294-2">Bipolar membrane water electrolysis maintains a large pH gradient so that anode and cathode processes can run under different pH; cheap OER catalysts can be used at the anode (basic) and Pt‑based HER catalysts at the cathode (acidic)</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-3">Key challenges include the overpotential of water dissociation at the bipolar junction and limited water transport to the interface; strategies include introducing mono/bilayer water‑dissociation catalysts at the junction and developing robust, thin, low‑crossover membranes to enhance water and ion transport while maintaining stability</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-1">Early electrochemical ED‑R concepts evolved into BPM‑based designs with multiple stacks that exploit pH swings from water splitting at the anode/cathode to regenerate alkaline hydroxides and capture CO2 at the anode during OER, with hydrogen evolved at the cathode during HER</cite>.

Electrode kinetics and system voltage: how membrane‑driven WS shapes the cell
The total voltage of an ED/EDR cell must overcome the thermodynamic minimum of 1.23 V plus kinetic and transport overpotentials at both electrodes, with OER typically dominating. <cite id="6392c2ab-1">The inherent HER/OER potential drop is 1.23 V, but initiation potentials exceed this; overpotentials follow Tafel behavior and add to give a total cell voltage above 1.23 V, with anode overpotentials often larger than cathode overpotentials</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-4">Because OER proceeds via a multistep, four‑electron pathway with sluggish kinetics, it is commonly the rate‑determining step and the primary bottleneck for efficiency</cite>. Membrane‑interface water splitting can influence the effective electrode overpotentials by supplying additional H+ to the cathode or OH− to the anode in the quasi‑equilibrium surface layers and by buffering pH and charge near the electrodes, thereby modifying the local reaction kinetics and mass transport. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">Including the water‑ion transport current in the model shows that WS‑generated H+ and OH− can significantly alter the distribution of ions and fields near the interface, with consequences for transport resistances and current efficiency</cite>. Conversely, excessive WS at AEMs can reduce efficiency by causing precipitation of sparingly soluble salts and by partially suppressing electroconvection, highlighting the need to tune membrane kinetics and boundary‑layer transport. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">WS is often undesirable because it reduces current efficiency and can precipitate sparingly soluble compounds; EC enhances ion transport but WS partially suppresses it</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-0">Reducing WS at AEMs while enhancing CEM electroconvection is key to improving overlimiting ED</cite>.

Design levers that connect membrane water splitting to electrode electrolysis
- Membrane chemistry and surface modification: <cite id="1b7a0116-0">Lowering water splitting rates at AEM surfaces is a key improvement for overlimiting ED</cite>, while <cite id="1b7a0116-4">AEMs inherently show stronger catalytic WS than CEMs due to charged sites; non‑catalytic WS occurs in strong fields of expanded space‑charge layers</cite>. Surface functionalization can suppress or tune these surface reactions to control interfacial charge and gas evolution.
- Electrode/electrochemistry: <cite id="6392c2ab-1">HER and OER overpotentials can be modeled via Tafel slopes and exchange current densities, and materials selection directly impacts the effective voltage</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-4">Rational catalyst design targets the sluggish OER to reduce the anode potential</cite>.
- Transport engineering: <cite id="1b7a0116-1">Electroconvection in CEMs enhances salt ion transport, but can be partially suppressed by WS at AEMs; balancing these phenomena is essential at high current densities</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-3">Impedance signatures show distinct contributions from WS at AEM/solution and at bipolar junctions, guiding interfacial engineering</cite>.
- Bipolar‑membrane stacks and EDR: <cite id="6392c2ab-3">Polarity reversal in EDR switches which electrodes oxidize and reduce, distributing electrolysis duty between anode and cathode over time</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-2">BPM stacks maintain large pH gradients so that OER/HER occur under optimal pH, reducing voltage relative to single‑compartment electrolysis</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-3">Catalysts at the BPM junction and robust membranes with thin, low‑crossover junctions improve water dissociation kinetics and mass transport</cite>.

Putting it together: the mechanistic picture
In ED/EDR, the applied potential establishes an electrochemical gradient that drives ion transport through alternating CEM/AEM, building space‑charge layers and strong fields in depleted boundary layers near membrane surfaces. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">These fields trigger water splitting at the membrane interfaces, generating H+ and OH− that migrate across the membranes and participate in HER/OER at the electrodes</cite>. Membrane water splitting thus “drives” electrolysis by providing the interfacial protons/hydroxides that neutralize local charge, buffer pH, and supply reactants to the electrode reactions, while the external electrodes supply or accept electrons to complete HER and OER. <cite id="6392c2ab-1">HER at the cathode and OER at the anode impose a baseline voltage of 1.23 V plus kinetic overpotentials that determine the overall cell voltage</cite>. In ED‑R, periodic polarity reversal alternately makes each electrode oxidizing or reducing, so that one side evolves O2 while the other evolves H2 in successive intervals; membrane‑interface WS supports both steps by supplying the corresponding counter‑ions near the electrodes. <cite id="6392c2ab-3">Polarity reversal increases recovery and extends membrane life</cite>. When BPMs are used, the junction‑localized water splitting supplies H+ to the cathode compartment and OH− to the anode compartment under a built‑in field, enabling optimal, separate pH for HER and OER and lowering the system voltage for water electrolysis. <cite id="2247b294-2">Bipolar membranes generate H+ and OH− at the junction and sustain large pH gradients that allow tailored catalysts on each side</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-4">The strong field and junction catalysts accelerate water dissociation, enabling efficient H2/O2 evolution under appropriate pH</cite>.

Practical implications and trade‑offs
Optimizing ED/EDR requires a balance among membrane water‑splitting rates, electroconvection, electrode kinetics, and mass transport to maximize current efficiency and minimize voltage. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">WS can enhance transport but cause precipitation and reduce efficiency; EC can boost ion flux yet is partly suppressed by WS</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-0">Reducing WS at AEMs while enhancing CEM electroconvection synergistically improves overlimiting ED</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-3">In bipolar systems, overpotential at the water‑splitting junction and limited water transport are major bottlenecks, motivating catalyst incorporation and membrane thinning to improve junction access</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-1">Accounting for HER/OER kinetics via Tafel parameters and exchange currents allows quantitative prediction of required overpotentials and effective cell voltage</cite>. Together, these insights explain how water splitting at ion‑exchange membranes physically and electrochemically couples to electrode reactions to drive electrolysis within ED/EDR stacks, and how materials and process choices govern efficiency and stability. <cite id="1b7a0116-4">The coexistence of catalytic and non‑catalytic WS mechanisms across AEM/CEM surfaces and in expanded space‑charge regions underpins both the enabling transport and the kinetic trade‑offs that must be engineered</cite>.

Snippet: In contrast, bipolar membrane water electrolysis allows a large pH gradient to be maintained across the electrolyzer, so that the anode and cathode processes can run at completely different pH. It is the nature of the bipolar membrane that allows this. A bipolar membrane consists of two ion-exchange polymers: an anion exchange layer composed of anionic (e.g. quaternary ammoniumbearing) headgroups and a cation exchange layer composed of cationic (e.g. sulfonic acid-bearing) headgroups. The anion exchange layer allows the permeation of OH − ions, whilst the cation exchange layer allows the permeation of H + , with these two ions being generated by the water dissociation process taking place at the interface between the two ion-exchange layers (Fig. 3) [21]. This extreme pH gradient presents opportunities for optimizing the types of catalysts used on each side of the electrolyzer. Cheap, earth-abundant oxygen evolution catalysts can be used at the anode in combination with highly-active Pt-based catalysts at the cathode, with the anode and cathode electrocatalysts each operating under the pH regime in which they work best [23]. 

In bipolar membrane water electrolysis, the hydrogen evolution reaction has a minimum theoretical onset potential of 0 V vs. SHE (at pH = 0) and the oxygen evolution reaction's onset potential is +0.404 V vs SHE (at pH = 14).

Title: Zero-Gap Bipolar Membrane Water Electrolyzers: Principles, Challenges and Practical Insights
Snippet: In this review, the theory of the bipolar membrane water electrolysis has been summarized and the advantages of implementing such a technology for producing hydrogen have been discussed. Due to the ability to maintain the anode and cathode compartments at different pH in this setup, highly efficient oxygen and hydrogen evolution reaction catalysts can be used in their most kinetically favorable conditions: high-pH and low-pH electrolytes for the oxygen and hydrogen evolution reactions, respectively. 

A number of key challenges remain in the development of this technology. The overpotential of the water dissociation reaction taking place at the bipolar junction and the limited water transport to the bipolar interface are the two major issues for this technology. In addition, operating a bipolar membrane water electrolyzer for a long period of time with a stable pH gradient is problematic due to ion crossover. 

The strategies adopted in the literature for improving bipolar membrane water electrolysis have been examined. Introducing water dissociation mono/bilayer catalysts placed at the bipolar junction has shown great promotion of the water dissociation process by reducing the water dissociation overpotential [35,40]. Moreover, developing robust bipolar membranes in extreme acidic and basic conditions, with high ionic exchange capacity, low thickness, limited ion crossover, and efficient water transport is crucial. Additionally, combining novel bipolar membranes with water dissociation catalysts between their anion and cation exchange layers is highly recommended for improved performance. Furthermore, thinning the anion and cation exchange layers at the bipolar junction could improve the water transport to, and the transport of protons and hydroxide ions away from, the bipolar junction, boosting the overall performance [36,41,48]. However, thinning the ion exchange layers might increase ion crossover, reducing overall electrolyzer efficiency, which can be mitigated by operating the electrolyzers at high current density [42]. 

Ultimately, emphasizing the importance of adhering to a standardized procedure/protocol is important when developing new membranes or performance-enhancing strategies, ensuring a consistent basis for comparison across different studies. For example, an assembling and testing protocol for a bipolar membrane water electrolyzer device was provided by Amador et al., offering step-by-step instructions for component fabrication and operational steps.

Title: A Standard Electrolyzer Test Cell Design for Evaluating Catalysts and Cell Components for Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis
Snippet: Anion exchange membrane water electrolysis technology is an environmentally friendly method for hydrogen production without carbon dioxide emissions. The development of this technology is hindered by the sluggish rates of the hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions, demanding the rational design of electrocatalysts for these processes. Although numerous hydrogen and oxygen evolution electrocatalysts are reported in the literature, there is currently no standard set of conditions or cell design under which they can be tested; variance in testing conditions and water electrolyzer components from one study to another therefore hampers a full and coherent comparison of novel electrocatalysts for anion exchange membrane water electrolysis. Herein, a standard water electrolyzer test cell was designed and optimized, such that this test cell can be adopted as a universal framework for evaluating novel electrocatalysts (and indeed other cell components) for anion exchange membrane water electrolysis. The performance of this water electrolyzer was evaluated using a commercial Pt/C hydrogen evolution reaction electrocatalyst, with an optimized cell found to deliver current densities of 1.40 A cm – 2 and 2.74 A cm – 2 at cell voltages of 2.0 V and at 60 ◦ C using Fumasep FAA-3-50 and Sustainion ® X37-50 membranes, respectively. Guidance for assembling and operating the water electrolyzer is provided, along with computer-aided design drawings of the electrolyzer and its components to allow others to construct their own identical cells for benchmarking catalysts and other cell components for anion exchange membrane water electrolysis.
</snippet>
