Title: Village-Scale Electrodialysis Desalination: Field Trial Validation
Snippet: In the electrodialysis (ED) process, saline water is pumped between a series of alternating anion and cation ion exchange membranes (AEM, CEM). A voltage potential is applied at an anode and cathode located at either end of the membrane stack (Figure 2). Anions move toward the anode and cations move toward the cathode due to the potential difference at the electrodes. However, anions are blocked when they reach the first CEM and thus remain in the concentrate compartment. Similarly, cations moving towards the cathode are blocked when they reach the first AEM. In a commercial ED stack, there are many alternating CEM and AEM membranes (each set is called a "cell pair"), resulting in alternating streams of diluted and concentrated saline flow. 

EDR uses the same stack arrangement as ED but reverses the polarity of the stack at certain time intervals. Polarity reversal increases membrane life by reducing fouling and allows for higher water recoveries to be achieved. This article describes a prototype PV-EDR system, designed, built and tested as part of the USAID Desal Prize. The goal of the prize aligned well with our research objectives: to design and characterize cost-effective, energy efficient, environmentally sustainable desalination technologies. Our system was designed to enable testing of a variety of groundwater compositions, with a production rate of 1.6 m 3 /hour. The goal of building and testing the prototype was: 1) to validate the technology's ability to achieve the desired water recovery and product water quality, 2) to validate the theoretical performance model, and 3) to identify potential challenges in making a commercially feasible solution for villages. 

To our knowledge, no published literature exists on the field-testing of village-scale PV-EDR systems. While work has been completed on the use of ED in remote areas [6,7] and on pairing ED with PV power [8], the work has thus far remained at the laboratory scale only. Adiga et. al. completed a pilot PV-ED project with a production rate of 0.12m 3 /hr in the Thar Desert (1987) [9].
</snippet>

Title: Decoding heterogeneous electrocatalysts for acidic oxygen evolution: mechanisms, rational design and AI acceleration
Snippet: Hydrogen is regarded as a valuable energy carrier and a promising alternative to traditional fossil fuels due to its sustainable characteristics and environmentally benign nature [1 ]. Currently, hydrogen is primarily produced through natural gas reforming and electrochemical water splitting. Among these, water electrolysis driven by renewable energy sources has gained increasing attention owing to its sustainability advantages [2 ]. In the electrochemical water splitting process, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) occurs at the cathode through a two-electron transfer mechanism, while the anode undergoes the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) involving a more intricate four-electron transfer process coupled with multiple proton-electron interactions [3 -8 ]. This fundamental difference in reaction mechanisms results in inherently sluggish reaction kinetics and elevated overpotential requirements for the OER compared to the HER [9 ]. Consequently, the OER has been identified as the rate-determining step (RDS) in water electrolysis systems, constituting a critical bottleneck in overall energy conversion efficiency. 

Recent water electrolysis technologies have primarily focused on proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs) and anion exchange membrane water electrolyzers (AEMWEs), as they can produce high-purity hydrogen compared to conventional alkaline water electrolyzers [10 ]. Among these, PEMWEs have a longer development history and exhibit technical maturity in several key parameters (Fig. 1 a). For example, commercial advanced  proton exchange membranes (PEMs) sti l l offer superior ionic conductivity ( ∼100 mS cm −1 ) compared with anion exchange membranes (AEMs). 

The well-established PEM technology also reduces membrane costs and extends the overall stack lifetime relative to AEMWEs. Moreover, the PEMWE electrolyte consists of pure water or acidic aqueous solutions (H 2 SO 4 , HClO 4 ), which provides advantages in applications that require strict pH control, compared with AEMWEs that rely on alkaline electrolytes. PEMWEs also demonstrate faster startup and shutdown response times (typically < 10 s) [11 ], enabling better compatibility with intermittent renewable energy sources such as wind and solar power.

Below is a mechanistic view of how water splitting at ion‑exchange membranes (IEMs) couples to electrolysis at the electrodes in electrodialysis (ED) and related modes.

Overview: ED stacks and electrodes
In ED, an anode and cathode apply a potential across alternating cation‑exchange (CEM) and anion‑exchange membranes (AEM), driving cations to the cathode and anions to the anode; transport is limited by diffusion/adsorption at selective interfaces and by electric fields and convection in the boundary layers near membranes. <cite id="1b7a0116-3">Anions move toward the anode and cations toward the cathode, but are blocked at the first selective membrane they meet, creating a sequence of diluted and concentrated compartments in a stack of alternating CEM/AEM</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-3">Polarity reversal (EDR) flips the stack to increase membrane life and achieve higher recoveries</cite>. At the electrodes, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) at the cathode and oxygen evolution reaction (OER) at the anode define the minimum thermodynamic driving force of about 1.23 V and impose additional overpotentials that depend on kinetics and mass transport. <cite id="6392c2ab-1">In ED, the hydrogen evolution reaction occurs at the cathode and the oxygen evolution reaction at the anode; the inherent potential drop is 1.23 V, but the actual initiation potential is higher, with overpotentials calculable via Tafel behavior</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-4">HER proceeds via a two‑electron transfer in alkaline AEMWE, whereas OER involves a four‑electron process with multiple proton–electron steps and sluggish kinetics, often rate‑limiting</cite>.

Water splitting at ion‑exchange membranes: catalytic and field‑driven mechanisms
Under moderate to high current densities, water can split at the surfaces and interfaces of IEMs, generating mobile H+ and OH− that affect ion transport and current efficiency. <cite id="1b7a0116-4">Water splitting in systems with IEMs is observed and arises from two mechanisms: catalytic dissociation/association on membrane ionic sites (proton transport between charged groups on AEMs) and non‑catalytic, field‑limited dissociation in expanded space‑charge regions where electric fields reach values that pull H and OH apart at maximum speed; WS is stronger on AEMs than CEMs</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-0">Decreasing water splitting rate at anion‑exchange membranes is key to improving overlimiting ED; a synergistic improvement arises when CEMs are optimized to enhance electroconvection and AEMs are optimized to suppress unwanted WS</cite>. At the microscopic scale near membranes, partial charge equilibrium breaks down in depleted diffusion layers, enabling coupled WS and ion transport to carry current; models based on the Nernst–Planck–Poisson framework capture how H+/OH− generated by WS modify fields and ion fluxes and why WS can both aid transport and reduce efficiency by promoting precipitation. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">Water splitting and electroconvection are the main phenomena affecting ion transfer in intensive current regimes; models that couple Nernst–Planck and Poisson equations across an electroneutral region, expanded space‑charge region, and quasi‑equilibrium surface zone reproduce ion concentrations and potential drops and show that, under the same current density, the surface space‑charge density at an AEM is lower than at a CEM, explaining how WS partially suppresses electroconvection and reduces salt ion transfer while transporting H+/OH−</cite>. Electrochemical impedance analyses also identify distinct electrical signatures of WS at AEM/solution and bipolar junctions. <cite id="1b7a0116-3">One sub‑arc corresponds to water splitting at the AEM/depleted solution interface, and another to water splitting at the bipolar junction</cite>.

How water splitting at membranes drives electrolysis at the electrodes
1) Charge accumulation and depletion near electrodes trigger WS and electrolysis. As cations accumulate at the cathode and anions at the anode under applied bias, local space‑charge and strong electric fields develop in depleted boundary layers, which can activate both catalytic and non‑catalytic WS. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">In the depleted diffusion boundary layer near an IEM, partial local electroneutrality breaks down, creating an expanded space‑charge region and quasi‑equilibrium surface zone where H+ and OH− generated by WS contribute to transport and modify the field structure</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-4">In such regions, fields can reach values sufficient to split water non‑catalytically at maximum speed, providing additional mobile carriers that screen charge and sustain current</cite>. These extra carriers couple to the electrode reactions: electrons supplied by the cathode reduce H+ (from WS or from migrated counterions) to H2 (HER), while electrons supplied to the anode oxidize OH− (from WS or from transported coions) to O2 (OER), thus manifesting electrolysis at the electrodes supported by membrane‑interface water splitting. <cite id="6392c2ab-1">The cathode HER and anode OER contribute potential drops whose thermodynamic minimum is 1.23 V and whose actual onset potentials exceed this value due to overpotentials that scale with current density via Tafel behavior</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-4">Because OER kinetics are intrinsically slower than HER, the anode often limits the overall cell voltage</cite>.

2) Coupled transport: membranes set directionality and selectivity that focus electrolysis where the field peaks. CEMs transmit H+ (or cations) and AEMs transmit OH− (or anions); under field reversal during EDR, roles swap. <cite id="6392c2ab-3">In ED, cations are blocked by the first AEM and anions by the first CEM; in EDR, polarity reversal of the stack allows net transport of counterions to the opposite electrodes and higher recoveries</cite>. Because membrane permselectivity and boundary‑layer depletion create strong internal fields near interfaces, the water splitting that occurs in the quasi‑equilibrium surface zones and bipolar regions supplies the mobile protons and hydroxides that neutralize local charge and shuttle to electrodes, where they participate in HER/OER and produce gas. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">A model that includes WS‑transported H+ and OH− across the depleted DBL shows how their current can be a significant fraction of total, even as WS reduces efficiency by precipitating sparingly soluble species</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-0">In overlimiting regimes, suppressing excessive WS at AEMs while enhancing CEM electroconvection is necessary to maintain high current without salt precipitation</cite>.

3) ED/EDR as intermittent electrolysis: polarity reversal alternately makes one electrode cathodic and anodic, so that each electrode periodically performs HER and OER. <cite id="6392c2ab-3">EDR reverses the polarity of the stack at set intervals; this extends membrane life and enables higher recoveries by periodically switching which side is anode and cathode</cite>. During the intervals when a given compartment is cathodic, cations accumulate at that electrode and the opposite anode, driving O2 evolution there; during the next interval, roles reverse and H2 evolution predominates at the same electrode. Membrane water splitting at the interfaces adjacent to the now‑reversed anode/cathode supports the corresponding electrolysis step by supplying H+/OH− to stabilize current and buffer pH near the electrodes. <cite id="1b7a0116-4">Field‑driven non‑catalytic water dissociation in expanded space‑charge regions at the membrane surfaces enables rapid generation of H+ and OH− under high fields, which can assist current transport during polarity reversal</cite>.

Bipolar‑membrane configurations decouple and optimize water splitting at the electrodes
When bipolar membranes (BPMs) are introduced, a junction of cation‑ and anion‑exchange layers creates a built‑in depletion region and strong internal electric field that preferentially dissociates water at the “bipolar junction,” producing H+ and OH− that migrate into adjacent compartments. <cite id="2247b294-2">A bipolar membrane consists of a cation‑exchange and an anion‑exchange layer laminated together; the junction, or bipolar interface, acts like a p–n junction, generating a depletion region and large electric field where water dissociation catalysts, if present, accelerate the splitting to produce H+ and OH− that migrate to opposite sides, enabling highly acidic and basic compartments with a large pH gradient</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-4">Under reverse bias (CEL to cathode, AEL to anode), migrating ions first move into bulk, then water at the interfacial layer polarizes and dissociates to generate H+ and OH−, which diffuse into adjacent compartments to create acidic and basic environments; this allows distinct pH optimization for OER and HER and reduces overall cell voltage for water splitting</cite>. In this architecture, the membrane‑driven water dissociation at the junction provides the charge carriers that traverse the membranes, while the electrodes operate at their kinetically favorable pH: OER in a relatively mild‑oxidation potential basic environment and HER in an acidic environment, minimizing the extra potential required beyond 1.23 V. <cite id="2247b294-2">Bipolar membrane water electrolysis maintains a large pH gradient so that anode and cathode processes can run under different pH; cheap OER catalysts can be used at the anode (basic) and Pt‑based HER catalysts at the cathode (acidic)</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-3">Key challenges include the overpotential of water dissociation at the bipolar junction and limited water transport to the interface; strategies include introducing mono/bilayer water‑dissociation catalysts at the junction and developing robust, thin, low‑crossover membranes to enhance water and ion transport while maintaining stability</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-1">Early electrochemical ED‑R concepts evolved into BPM‑based designs with multiple stacks that exploit pH swings from water splitting at the anode/cathode to regenerate alkaline hydroxides and capture CO2 at the anode during OER, with hydrogen evolved at the cathode during HER</cite>.

Electrode kinetics and system voltage: how membrane‑driven WS shapes the cell
The total voltage of an ED/EDR cell must overcome the thermodynamic minimum of 1.23 V plus kinetic and transport overpotentials at both electrodes, with OER typically dominating. <cite id="6392c2ab-1">The inherent HER/OER potential drop is 1.23 V, but initiation potentials exceed this; overpotentials follow Tafel behavior and add to give a total cell voltage above 1.23 V, with anode overpotentials often larger than cathode overpotentials</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-4">Because OER proceeds via a multistep, four‑electron pathway with sluggish kinetics, it is commonly the rate‑determining step and the primary bottleneck for efficiency</cite>. Membrane‑interface water splitting can influence the effective electrode overpotentials by supplying additional H+ to the cathode or OH− to the anode in the quasi‑equilibrium surface layers and by buffering pH and charge near the electrodes, thereby modifying the local reaction kinetics and mass transport. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">Including the water‑ion transport current in the model shows that WS‑generated H+ and OH− can significantly alter the distribution of ions and fields near the interface, with consequences for transport resistances and current efficiency</cite>. Conversely, excessive WS at AEMs can reduce efficiency by causing precipitation of sparingly soluble salts and by partially suppressing electroconvection, highlighting the need to tune membrane kinetics and boundary‑layer transport. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">WS is often undesirable because it reduces current efficiency and can precipitate sparingly soluble compounds; EC enhances ion transport but WS partially suppresses it</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-0">Reducing WS at AEMs while enhancing CEM electroconvection is key to improving overlimiting ED</cite>.

Design levers that connect membrane water splitting to electrode electrolysis
- Membrane chemistry and surface modification: <cite id="1b7a0116-0">Lowering water splitting rates at AEM surfaces is a key improvement for overlimiting ED</cite>, while <cite id="1b7a0116-4">AEMs inherently show stronger catalytic WS than CEMs due to charged sites; non‑catalytic WS occurs in strong fields of expanded space‑charge layers</cite>. Surface functionalization can suppress or tune these surface reactions to control interfacial charge and gas evolution.
- Electrode/electrochemistry: <cite id="6392c2ab-1">HER and OER overpotentials can be modeled via Tafel slopes and exchange current densities, and materials selection directly impacts the effective voltage</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-4">Rational catalyst design targets the sluggish OER to reduce the anode potential</cite>.
- Transport engineering: <cite id="1b7a0116-1">Electroconvection in CEMs enhances salt ion transport, but can be partially suppressed by WS at AEMs; balancing these phenomena is essential at high current densities</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-3">Impedance signatures show distinct contributions from WS at AEM/solution and at bipolar junctions, guiding interfacial engineering</cite>.
- Bipolar‑membrane stacks and EDR: <cite id="6392c2ab-3">Polarity reversal in EDR switches which electrodes oxidize and reduce, distributing electrolysis duty between anode and cathode over time</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-2">BPM stacks maintain large pH gradients so that OER/HER occur under optimal pH, reducing voltage relative to single‑compartment electrolysis</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-3">Catalysts at the BPM junction and robust membranes with thin, low‑crossover junctions improve water dissociation kinetics and mass transport</cite>.

Putting it together: the mechanistic picture
In ED/EDR, the applied potential establishes an electrochemical gradient that drives ion transport through alternating CEM/AEM, building space‑charge layers and strong fields in depleted boundary layers near membrane surfaces. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">These fields trigger water splitting at the membrane interfaces, generating H+ and OH− that migrate across the membranes and participate in HER/OER at the electrodes</cite>. Membrane water splitting thus “drives” electrolysis by providing the interfacial protons/hydroxides that neutralize local charge, buffer pH, and supply reactants to the electrode reactions, while the external electrodes supply or accept electrons to complete HER and OER. <cite id="6392c2ab-1">HER at the cathode and OER at the anode impose a baseline voltage of 1.23 V plus kinetic overpotentials that determine the overall cell voltage</cite>. In ED‑R, periodic polarity reversal alternately makes each electrode oxidizing or reducing, so that one side evolves O2 while the other evolves H2 in successive intervals; membrane‑interface WS supports both steps by supplying the corresponding counter‑ions near the electrodes. <cite id="6392c2ab-3">Polarity reversal increases recovery and extends membrane life</cite>. When BPMs are used, the junction‑localized water splitting supplies H+ to the cathode compartment and OH− to the anode compartment under a built‑in field, enabling optimal, separate pH for HER and OER and lowering the system voltage for water electrolysis. <cite id="2247b294-2">Bipolar membranes generate H+ and OH− at the junction and sustain large pH gradients that allow tailored catalysts on each side</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-4">The strong field and junction catalysts accelerate water dissociation, enabling efficient H2/O2 evolution under appropriate pH</cite>.

Practical implications and trade‑offs
Optimizing ED/EDR requires a balance among membrane water‑splitting rates, electroconvection, electrode kinetics, and mass transport to maximize current efficiency and minimize voltage. <cite id="1b7a0116-1">WS can enhance transport but cause precipitation and reduce efficiency; EC can boost ion flux yet is partly suppressed by WS</cite>. <cite id="1b7a0116-0">Reducing WS at AEMs while enhancing CEM electroconvection synergistically improves overlimiting ED</cite>. <cite id="2247b294-3">In bipolar systems, overpotential at the water‑splitting junction and limited water transport are major bottlenecks, motivating catalyst incorporation and membrane thinning to improve junction access</cite>. <cite id="6392c2ab-1">Accounting for HER/OER kinetics via Tafel parameters and exchange currents allows quantitative prediction of required overpotentials and effective cell voltage</cite>. Together, these insights explain how water splitting at ion‑exchange membranes physically and electrochemically couples to electrode reactions to drive electrolysis within ED/EDR stacks, and how materials and process choices govern efficiency and stability. <cite id="1b7a0116-4">The coexistence of catalytic and non‑catalytic WS mechanisms across AEM/CEM surfaces and in expanded space‑charge regions underpins both the enabling transport and the kinetic trade‑offs that must be engineered</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Mathematical Modeling of the Effect of Water Splitting on Ion Transfer in the Depleted Diffusion Layer Near an Ion-Exchange Membrane
Snippet: Water splitting (WS) and electroconvection (EC) are the main phenomena affecting ion transfer through ion-exchange membranes in intensive current regimes of electrodialysis. While EC enhances ion transport, WS, in most cases, is an undesirable effect reducing current efficiency and causing precipitation of sparingly soluble compounds. A mathematical description of the transfer of salt ions and H+ (OH−) ions generated in WS is presented. The model is based on the Nernst–Planck and Poisson equations; it takes into account deviation from local electroneutrality in the depleted diffusion boundary layer (DBL). The current transported by water ions is given as a parameter. Numerical and semi-analytical solutions are developed. The analytical solution is found by dividing the depleted DBL into three zones: the electroneutral region, the extended space charge region (SCR), and the quasi-equilibrium zone near the membrane surface. There is an excellent agreement between two solutions when calculating the concentration of all four ions, electric field, and potential drop across the depleted DBL. The treatment of experimental partial current–voltage curves shows that under the same current density, the surface space charge density at the anion-exchange membrane is lower than that at the cation-exchange membrane. This explains the negative effect of WS, which partially suppresses EC and reduces salt ion transfer. The restrictions of the analytical solution, namely, the local chemical equilibrium assumption, are discussed.

Title: Theoretical Analysis of the Stationary Transport of 1:1 Salt Ions in a Cross-Section of a Desalination Channel, Taking into Account the Non-Catalytic Dissociation/Recombination Reaction of Water Molecules
Snippet: Electrodialysis is widely used in wastewater treatment processes, including for toxic heavy metal salts [1][2][3][4]. Since the cost of the electrodialysis process depends on the surface area of ion-exchange membranes, the maximum possible current densities are used to increase the efficiency of the process [5,6]. At the same time, it is known that at overlimiting current densities (the limiting current is hereinafter referred to as the limiting diffusion current [7]), many different phenomena occur, the main of which are the dissociation/recombination reaction of water molecules, the appearance of an expanded space charge region, which leads to the emergence and development of electroconvection [8], the main mechanism of overlimiting transport. 

Water splitting in systems with ion-exchange membranes was first observed by Frillett [9], as well as by Cressman and Tai [10], and has since been studied in articles [11][12][13][14]. Taking into account the effect of the dissociation/recombination reaction of water molecules is important for understanding the processes of ion transport in electromembrane systems, since the appearance of new charge carriers H + and OH − can lead to a decrease or even disappearance of the space charge. Currently, it is considered that there are two different mechanisms of water dissociation in electromembrane systems, namely, catalytic and non-catalytic. According to the catalytic mechanism of water dissociation on ion-exchange membranes, ions H + (OH − ) can occur in proton transport reactions between charged groups in the membrane and water molecules [15,16]. It was found that water dissociation is more pronounced on anion-exchange membranes (AEM) and less significant on cation-exchange membranes (CEM) [16]. In a number of works [17,18], we have shown that, in the expanded region of the space charge, the electric field intensity reaches such high values that it pulls apart the hydrogen and hydroxyl ions in this region and a non-catalytic reaction of dissociation of water molecules occurs at the maximum possible speed. 

The study of all these phenomena simultaneously presents a complex problem.

snippet.text:
Electrodialysis is widely used in wastewater treatment processes, including for toxic heavy metal salts [1][2][3][4]. Since the cost of the electrodialysis process depends on the surface area of ion-exchange membranes, the maximum possible current densities are used to increase the efficiency of the process [5,6]. At the same time, it is known that at overlimiting current densities (the limiting current is hereinafter referred to as the limiting diffusion current [7]), many different phenomena occur, the main of which are the dissociation/recombination reaction of water molecules, the appearance of an expanded space charge region, which leads to the emergence and development of electroconvection [8], the main mechanism of overlimiting transport. 

Water splitting in systems with ion-exchange membranes was first observed by Frillett [9], as well as by Cressman and Tai [10], and has since been studied in articles [11][12][13][14]. Taking into account the effect of the dissociation/recombination reaction of water molecules is important for understanding the processes of ion transport in electromembrane systems, since the appearance of new charge carriers H + and OH − can lead to a decrease or even disappearance of the space charge. Currently, it is considered that there are two different mechanisms of water dissociation in electromembrane systems, namely, catalytic and non-catalytic. According to the catalytic mechanism of water dissociation on ion-exchange membranes, ions H + (OH − ) can occur in proton transport reactions between charged groups in the membrane and water molecules [15,16]. It was found that water dissociation is more pronounced on anion-exchange membranes (AEM) and less significant on cation-exchange membranes (CEM) [16]. In a number of works [17,18], we have shown that, in the expanded region of the space charge, the electric field intensity reaches such high values that it pulls apart the hydrogen and hydroxyl ions in this region and a non-catalytic reaction of dissociation of water molecules occurs at the maximum possible speed. 

The study of all these phenomena simultaneously presents a complex problem.

documents.title: Mathematical Modeling of the Effect of Water Splitting on Ion Transfer in the Depleted Diffusion Layer Near an Ion-Exchange Membrane
documents.snippet: Water splitting (WS) and electroconvection (EC) are the main phenomena affecting ion transfer through ion-exchange membranes in intensive current regimes of electrodialysis. While EC enhances ion transport, WS, in most cases, is an undesirable effect reducing current efficiency and causing precipitation of sparingly soluble compounds. A mathematical description of the transfer of salt ions and H+ (OH−) ions generated in WS is presented. The model is based on the Nernst–Planck and Poisson equations; it takes into account deviation from local electroneutrality in the depleted diffusion boundary layer (DBL). The current transported by water ions is given as a parameter. Numerical and semi-analytical solutions are developed. The analytical solution is found by dividing the depleted DBL into three zones: the electroneutral region, the extended space charge region (SCR), and the quasi-equilibrium zone near the membrane surface. There is an excellent agreement between two solutions when calculating the concentration of all four ions, electric field, and potential drop across the depleted DBL. The treatment of experimental partial current–voltage curves shows that under the same current density, the surface space charge density at the anion-exchange membrane is lower than that at the cation-exchange membrane. This explains the negative effect of WS, which partially suppresses EC and reduces salt ion transfer. The restrictions of the analytical solution, namely, the local chemical equilibrium assumption, are discussed.

Title: Zero-Gap Bipolar Membrane Water Electrolyzers: Principles, Challenges and Practical Insights
Snippet: In contrast, bipolar membrane water electrolysis allows a large pH gradient to be maintained across the electrolyzer, so that the anode and cathode processes can run at completely different pH. It is the nature of the bipolar membrane that allows this. A bipolar membrane consists of two ion-exchange polymers: an anion exchange layer composed of anionic (e.g. quaternary ammoniumbearing) headgroups and a cation exchange layer composed of cationic (e.g. sulfonic acid-bearing) headgroups. The anion exchange layer allows the permeation of OH − ions, whilst the cation exchange layer allows the permeation of H + , with these two ions being generated by the water dissociation process taking place at the interface between the two ion-exchange layers (Fig. 3) [21]. This interfacial region located between two ion exchange layers is known as the bipolar junction or bipolar interface, with a thickness much lower than 0.1 μm, as shown in scanning electron microscopy images of a commercial bipolar membrane (Fig. 4) [22]. 

As the charge carriers are generated in the middle of the membrane and then migrate in opposite directions depending on their charge, bipolar membranes allow the cationic (cathode) side of the cell to be highly acidic, whilst the anionic (anode) side can be highly basic. This extreme pH gradient presents opportunities for optimizing the types of catalysts used on each side of the electrolyzer. Cheap, earth-abundant oxygen evolution catalysts can be used at the anode in combination with highly-active Pt-based catalysts at the cathode, with the anode and cathode electrocatalysts each operating under the pH regime in which they work best [23]. 

In bipolar membrane water electrolysis, the hydrogen evolution reaction has a minimum theoretical onset potential of 0 V vs. SHE (at pH = 0) and the oxygen evolution reaction's onset potential is +0.404 V vs SHE (at pH = 14).

Title: Zero-Gap Bipolar Membrane Water Electrolyzers: Principles, Challenges and Practical Insights
Snippet: In this review, the theory of the bipolar membrane water electrolysis has been summarized and the advantages of implementing such a technology for producing hydrogen have been discussed. Due to the ability to maintain the anode and cathode compartments at different pH in this setup, highly efficient oxygen and hydrogen evolution reaction catalysts can be used in their most kinetically favorable conditions: high-pH and low-pH electrolytes for the oxygen and hydrogen evolution reactions, respectively. 

A number of key challenges remain in the development of this technology. The overpotential of the water dissociation reaction taking place at the bipolar junction and the limited water transport to the bipolar interface are the two major issues for this technology. In addition, operating a bipolar membrane water electrolyzer for a long period of time with a stable pH gradient is problematic due to ion crossover. 

The strategies adopted in the literature for improving bipolar membrane water electrolysis have been examined. Introducing water dissociation mono/bilayer catalysts placed at the bipolar junction has shown great promotion of the water dissociation process by reducing the water dissociation overpotential [35,40]. Moreover, developing robust bipolar membranes in extreme acidic and basic conditions, with high ionic exchange capacity, low thickness, limited ion crossover, and efficient water transport is crucial. Additionally, combining novel bipolar membranes with water dissociation catalysts between their anion and cation exchange layers is highly recommended for improved performance. Furthermore, thinning the anion and cation exchange layers at the bipolar junction could improve the water transport to, and the transport of protons and hydroxide ions away from, the bipolar junction, boosting the overall performance [36,41,48]. However, thinning the ion exchange layers might increase ion crossover, reducing overall electrolyzer efficiency, which can be mitigated by operating the electrolyzers at high current density [42]. 

Ultimately, emphasizing the importance of adhering to a standardized procedure/protocol is important when developing new membranes or performance-enhancing strategies, ensuring a consistent basis for comparison across different studies. For example, an assembling and testing protocol for a bipolar membrane water electrolyzer device was provided by Amador et al., offering step-by-step instructions for component fabrication and operational steps.

By applying a reverse bias (CEL facing the cathode and AEL facing the anode), the ions at a bipolar or junction or interfacial layer, which is the junction of CEL and AEL, initially migrate to the bulk solution. 30 Subsequently, as the ions become depleted, water molecules at the interfacial layer undergo polarization and dissociation, generating H + and OH − ions. 31 These ions then move into adjacent solution compartments, creating an acidic and basic environment. By applying a reverse bias (CEL facing the cathode and AEL facing the anode), the ions at a bipolar or junction or interfacial layer, which is the junction of CEL and AEL, initially migrate to the bulk solution. 30 Subsequently, as the ions become depleted, water molecules at the interfacial layer undergo polarization and dissociation, generating H + and OH − ions. 31 These ions then move into adjacent solution compartments, creating an acidic and basic environment. Leveraging the unique water dissociation characteristics of the interfacial layer, the incorporation of BPMs in the electrochemical configuration allows for the maintenance of two distinct pH environments. 32 n contrast to traditional configurations, which must optimize electrode stability, catalyst activity, and cost at both the cathode and anode for a single pH, the BPM permits electrochemical devices in which optimum pH conditions can be determined individually for each half-reaction. 33 BPM allows hydrogen and oxygen evolution processes under appropriate pH conditions, reducing overall cell voltage for the water dissociation reaction. 34 The strong electric field at the interface and the presence of catalysts in the junction or interface of BPM are responsible for the acceleration of water dissociation. 30 longside the thermodynamic potential, the water dissociation potential of BPMs significantly impacts the system efficiency. 30 ecent research has shown that energy-saving hydrogen production by seawater electrolysis employing BPM results in low cell voltages and lower electricity use. 35 his paper comprehensively discusses the production of hydrogen from seawater by using BPMs. The discussion begins with an overview of various hydrogen production methods. It then delves into the mechanism of water splitting using bipolar membranes and the recent advancements in their fabrication. The final part of the discussion focuses on the BPM electrolysis performance in hydrogen production from seawater, limitations, and enhancement strategies. Then, the challenges and perspectives in this field are pointed out. production, accounting for the majority of global output. 38

Title: A Standard Electrolyzer Test Cell Design for Evaluating Catalysts and Cell Components for Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis
Snippet: Anion exchange membrane water electrolysis technology is an environmentally friendly method for hydrogen production without carbon dioxide emissions. The development of this technology is hindered by the sluggish rates of the hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions, demanding the rational design of electrocatalysts for these processes. Although numerous hydrogen and oxygen evolution electrocatalysts are reported in the literature, there is currently no standard set of conditions or cell design under which they can be tested; variance in testing conditions and water electrolyzer components from one study to another therefore hampers a full and coherent comparison of novel electrocatalysts for anion exchange membrane water electrolysis. Herein, a standard water electrolyzer test cell was designed and optimized, such that this test cell can be adopted as a universal framework for evaluating novel electrocatalysts (and indeed other cell components) for anion exchange membrane water electrolysis. The performance of this water electrolyzer was evaluated using a commercial Pt/C hydrogen evolution reaction electrocatalyst, with an optimized cell found to deliver current densities of 1.40 A cm – 2 and 2.74 A cm – 2 at cell voltages of 2.0 V and at 60 ◦ C using Fumasep FAA-3-50 and Sustainion ® X37-50 membranes, respectively. Guidance for assembling and operating the water electrolyzer is provided, along with computer-aided design drawings of the electrolyzer and its components to allow others to construct their own identical cells for benchmarking catalysts and other cell components for anion exchange membrane water electrolysis.

Title: Village-Scale Electrodialysis Desalination: Field Trial Validation
Snippet: In the electrodialysis (ED) process, saline water is pumped between a series of alternating anion and cation ion exchange membranes (AEM, CEM). A voltage potential is applied at an anode and cathode located at either end of the membrane stack (Figure 2). Anions move toward the anode and cations move toward the cathode due to the potential difference at the electrodes. However, anions are blocked when they reach the first CEM and thus remain in the concentrate compartment. Similarly, cations moving towards the cathode are blocked when they reach the first AEM. In a commercial ED stack, there are many alternating CEM and AEM membranes (each set is called a "cell pair"), resulting in alternating streams of diluted and concentrated saline flow. 

EDR uses the same stack arrangement as ED but reverses the polarity of the stack at certain time intervals. Polarity reversal increases membrane life by reducing fouling and allows for higher water recoveries to be achieved. This article describes a prototype PV-EDR system, designed, built and tested as part of the USAID Desal Prize. The goal of the prize aligned well with our research objectives: to design and characterize cost-effective, energy efficient, environmentally sustainable desalination technologies. Our system was designed to enable testing of a variety of groundwater compositions, with a production rate of 1.6 m 3 /hour. The goal of building and testing the prototype was: 1) to validate the technology's ability to achieve the desired water recovery and product water quality, 2) to validate the theoretical performance model, and 3) to identify potential challenges in making a commercially feasible solution for villages. 

To our knowledge, no published literature exists on the field-testing of village-scale PV-EDR systems. While work has been completed on the use of ED in remote areas [6,7] and on pairing ED with PV power [8], the work has thus far remained at the laboratory scale only. Adiga et. al. completed a pilot PV-ED project with a production rate of 0.12m 3 /hr in the Thar Desert (1987) [9].

Title: Decoding heterogeneous electrocatalysts for acidic oxygen evolution: mechanisms, rational design and AI acceleration
Snippet: Hydrogen is regarded as a valuable energy carrier and a promising alternative to traditional fossil fuels due to its sustainable characteristics and environmentally benign nature [1 ]. Currently, hydrogen is primarily produced through natural gas reforming and electrochemical water splitting. Among these, water electrolysis driven by renewable energy sources has gained increasing attention owing to its sustainability advantages [2 ]. In the electrochemical water splitting process, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) occurs at the cathode through a two-electron transfer mechanism, while the anode undergoes the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) involving a more intricate four-electron transfer process coupled with multiple proton-electron interactions [3 -8 ]. This fundamental difference in reaction mechanisms results in inherently sluggish reaction kinetics and elevated overpotential requirements for the OER compared to the HER [9 ]. Consequently, the OER has been identified as the rate-determining step (RDS) in water electrolysis systems, constituting a critical bottleneck in overall energy conversion efficiency. 

Recent water electrolysis technologies have primarily focused on proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs) and anion exchange membrane water electrolyzers (AEMWEs), as they can produce high-purity hydrogen compared to conventional alkaline water electrolyzers [10 ]. Among these, PEMWEs have a longer development history and exhibit technical maturity in several key parameters (Fig. 1 a). For example, commercial advanced  proton exchange membranes (PEMs) sti l l offer superior ionic conductivity ( ∼100 mS cm −1 ) compared with anion exchange membranes (AEMs). 

The well-established PEM technology also reduces membrane costs and extends the overall stack lifetime relative to AEMWEs. Moreover, the PEMWE electrolyte consists of pure water or acidic aqueous solutions (H 2 SO 4 , HClO 4 ), which provides advantages in applications that require strict pH control, compared with AEMWEs that rely on alkaline electrolytes. PEMWEs also demonstrate faster startup and shutdown response times (typically < 10 s) [11 ], enabling better compatibility with intermittent renewable energy sources such as wind and solar power.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer fundamentally fails the verification criterion by treating membrane water splitting and electrode electrolysis as causally linked processes rather than as distinct, independent phenomena. Throughout the answer, it explicitly claims that membrane water splitting 'drives' electrolysis at the electrodes. For example: 'Membrane water splitting thus "drives" electrolysis by providing the interfacial protons/hydroxides that neutralize local charge, buffer pH, and supply reactants to the electrode reactions' and the section titled 'How water splitting at membranes drives electrolysis at the electrodes' describes a causal mechanism. The answer should have rejected the premise by clarifying that (1) membrane water splitting is a phenomenon caused by concentration polarization at ion-exchange membranes throughout the ED stack, and (2) electrode electrolysis is driven independently by the applied voltage causing redox reactions at the terminal electrodes. Instead, the answer accepts and elaborates on the false premise that one process drives the other.
other_issues: Conflates two entirely separate processes: water splitting at IEMs (a transport/concentration polarization phenomenon occurring at membranes throughout the stack) with water electrolysis at electrodes (redox reactions at anode/cathode)

Incorrectly suggests that H+ and OH- generated at membrane interfaces 'supply reactants to the electrode reactions' as if this were necessary for electrolysis to occur - electrode reactions split water molecules at the electrode surface itself

The discussion of bipolar membranes, while potentially accurate in that context, further confuses the issue by introducing a different system architecture where water splitting at a membrane junction is intentionally used in water electrolysis applications
Treats EDR (electrodialysis reversal) as 'intermittent electrolysis' when it is actually a periodic polarity reversal technique for desalination, not a method of water electrolysis
The answer appears to blend concepts from standard electrodialysis (ion separation) with bipolar membrane water electrolysis (hydrogen production), creating a confused mechanistic picture
judgment.summary: The answer completely fails to reject the false premise embedded in the question. Instead of clarifying that membrane water splitting and electrode electrolysis are independent processes with different causes and locations, it elaborates an incorrect causal mechanism linking them. The answer conflates concentration polarization effects at membranes with electrode redox chemistry, and further confuses the issue by mixing standard ED concepts with bipolar membrane electrolysis applications. This represents a fundamental misunderstanding or misrepresentation of the distinct physical phenomena involved.
